His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people﴾, meaning: who befriended them.

Qatadah said: They are the hypocrites, who allied themselves with the Jews.

al-Suddi and Muqatil said: They are the Jews, who allied themselves with the hypocrites. The first view is supported by His saying, "Allah has become wrathful toward them," since those upon whom wrath falls are the Jews. The second view is supported by His saying, ﴿neither of you nor of them﴾, since this is the description of the hypocrites, as Allah said of them: "wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those" [An-Nisa: 143]. The clause ﴿neither of you nor of them﴾ is either in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new independent sentence. ﴿And they swear falsely﴾, meaning they swear that they are Muslims, or they swear that they did not convey news to the Jews. This clause is coordinated with "took as allies" and falls under the sense of wonder at their act. The clause ﴿while they know﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: while they know the falsehood of what they swore to, and that it is a lie with no reality.

﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾, because of this alliance and this swearing to falsehood. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾, of ugly deeds.

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾. The majority of readers recited "aymanahum" with a fatha on the hamza, plural of yamin (oath), which refers to the false oaths they swore that they were among the Muslims, to protect themselves from being killed. Thus they made these oaths a protection and a covering in front of their blood, just as a fighter takes a shield as protection against being struck by a sword, a spear, or an arrow. [p. 1471]

al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah recited "imanahum" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning they made their affirmation of faith a shield from being killed. Thus their tongues professed faith out of fear of being killed, while their hearts did not believe. ﴿So they averted [others] from the way of Allah﴾, meaning they prevented people from Islam through what proceeded from them of discouragement, belittling the affair of the Muslims, and weakening their strength. It was also said that the meaning is: they turned the Muslims away from fighting them, by means of their showing Islam. ﴿So for them is a humiliating punishment﴾, meaning it humiliates and disgraces them. It was said that this is a repetition of His saying, ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾, for emphasis. It was also said that the first is the punishment of the grave and this is the punishment of the Hereafter, but there is no basis for the view of repetition, for the punishment described as severe is other than the punishment described as humiliating.

﴿Their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾, meaning their wealth and children will not avail them against His punishment in any way at all.

Muqatil said: The hypocrites said, "Muhammad claims that he will be helped on the Day of Resurrection. If so, we have certainly been wretched. By Allah, we will surely be helped on the Day of Resurrection with our selves, our wealth, and our children, if there is indeed a Resurrection." Then this verse was revealed.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning those described as mentioned, who will not leave it, ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾, meaning they will not come out of it.

﴿The Day when Allah will resurrect them all﴾: the time expression is in the accusative, governed by "humiliating," or by an implied verb, meaning: remember. ﴿Then they will swear to Him as they swear to you﴾, meaning they will swear to Allah on the Day of Resurrection falsely, as they swore to you in this world. This is due to the extreme of their wretchedness and the increased sealing over their hearts, for on the Day of Resurrection the realities will have been revealed and matters will be known by necessary direct witnessing. So how do they dare to lie in that station and swear falsely? ﴿And they think that they are upon something﴾, meaning they think in the Hereafter that by those false oaths they are upon something that brings benefit or repels harm, as they used to think in this world. ﴿Unquestionably, they are the liars﴾, meaning the complete ones in lying, who are thoroughly devoted to it, reaching such a degree that others have not reached it, by their boldness in it and in false oaths at the standing of the Resurrection before the Most Merciful.

﴿Satan has overcome them﴾, meaning he prevailed over them, rose above them, and took control.

al-Mubarrad said: "Istahwadha 'ala al-shay'" means he gathered it and encompassed it. It was also said: he became strong over them. It was said: he gathered them. One says "ahwadha al-shay'", meaning he gathered it and joined some of it to another. The meanings are close, because when he gathers them, he has become strong over them, overcome them, risen above them, taken control of them, and encompassed them.

﴿So he made them forget the remembrance of Allah﴾, meaning His commands and acting in obedience to Him, so they did not remember any of that. It was said: His prohibitions against His disobediences. It was also said: they did not remember Him with their hearts nor with their tongues. The indication by His saying "those" refers to those mentioned, described by those attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿the party of Satan﴾, meaning his soldiers, followers, and kin. ﴿Unquestionably, the party of Satan are the losers﴾, meaning the complete ones in loss, to the extent that the loss of others, compared to their loss, is not a loss, for they sold Paradise and guidance for misguidance, lied against Allah and His Prophet, and swore false oaths in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾: the meaning of opposition to Allah and His Messenger has been mentioned at the beginning of this surah. The sentence is an explanation of what precedes it, "those [among] the most humiliated," meaning: those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, described by the attributes mentioned earlier, are among those whom Allah has humiliated from the previous and later nations, because when they opposed Allah and His Messenger, they came to this place of humiliation.

Ata said: He means humiliation in this world and disgrace in the Hereafter.

"Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail." The sentence is independent, to confirm what precedes it along with their being among the most humiliated. Meaning: He wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) and decreed it in His prior knowledge: ﴿I will surely prevail, I and My messengers﴾, by argument and by sword.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the messengers' prevailing is of two kinds: whoever was sent among them with war prevails in war, and whoever was sent among them without war prevails by argument.

al-Farra' said: "Kataba" means "qala" (said), and His saying "ana" is for emphasis. Then he mentioned the like of al-Zajjaj's statement. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾: He is strong in supporting His allies and prevailing over His enemies, and no one can overcome Him.

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it, meaning: they love and befriend those who are hostile to Allah and His Messenger and oppose them both. The clause ﴿loving﴾ is in a position of accusative as a second object of "you will find" if it is transitive to two objects, or in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause if it is transitive to one object, or it is another attribute of "a people," meaning: they combine faith with love for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. ﴿Even if they were their fathers, or their sons, or their brothers, or their clan﴾, meaning even if those opposing Allah and His Messenger were the fathers of those who love them. Faith restrains and prevents one from that, and its safeguarding is stronger than the safeguarding of fatherhood, sonship, brotherhood, and kinship.

﴿Those — He has written faith into their hearts﴾, meaning those who do not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. The meaning of ﴿He has written faith into their hearts﴾ is: He created it. It was said: He established it. It was said: He made it. It was said: He gathered it. The meanings are close. ﴿And He supported them with a spirit from Him﴾, meaning He strengthened them with help from Him against their enemy in this world. He called His help "spirit" because by it their affair lives. It was said that it is the light of the heart.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: By the Qur'an and the argument. It was said: by Jibril. It was said: by faith. It was said: by mercy.

The majority recited "kataba" in the active voice, with "al-iman" in the accusative as the object.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim recited it in the passive voice, with "al-iman" in the nominative as the substitute subject.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh recited "'ashiratuhum" in the plural, and this reading is narrated from 'Asim.

﴿And He will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, meaning eternally. ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾, meaning He accepted their deeds and poured upon them the traces of His mercy, both immediate and deferred. ﴿And they are pleased with Him﴾, meaning they rejoiced in what He gave them, both immediate and deferred. ﴿Those are the party of Allah﴾, meaning His soldiers, who carry out His commands, fight His enemies, and support His allies. In attributing them to Allah, the Exalted, there is great honor for them and magnificent dignity. ﴿Unquestionably, the party of Allah — they are the successful﴾, meaning those who win the happiness of this world and the Hereafter, complete in success, whose success has become the perfect single example, so that the success of others, compared to their success, is no success at all.

[p. 1472] Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting in the shade of one of his chambers, and with him was a group of Muslims. He said: 'A man will soon come to you who will look at you with the eye of a devil. When he comes, do not speak to him.' They had not waited long when a blue-eyed man appeared to them. When he saw him, he said: 'Why do you and your companions revile me?' He said: 'Leave me, and I will bring them to you.' Then they swore and made excuses, and Allah revealed: ﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and they will swear to Him as they swear to you﴾, and the verse that follows it."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shawdhab, who said: The father of Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah began targeting Abu 'Ubaydah on the day of Badr, and Abu 'Ubaydah kept turning away from him. When he persisted, Abu 'Ubaydah confronted him and killed him. Then this was revealed: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah﴾, the verse.

Its revelation place is Medinan.

Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Surat al-Hashr was revealed in Medina.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas, "Surat al-Hashr?" He said, "Surat al-Nadir." He meant that it was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir, as he stated explicitly in some narrations.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The exegesis of this has already been given in Surat al-Hadid.

﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering.﴾ They are the Banu al-Nadir, a group of Jews of the descendants of Harun (Aaron). They settled in Medina during the trials of the Children of Israel, expecting Muhammad ﷺ. They betrayed the Prophet ﷺ after they had made a covenant with him, and sided with the polytheists against him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ besieged them until they agreed to leave.

al-Kalbi said: They were the first of the protected people (dhimmis, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection) to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula. Then the last of them were expelled in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. Their expulsion was thus the first gathering from Medina, and ʿUmar's expulsion of them was the last gathering.

It was also said that the first gathering was their removal from their fortresses to Khaybar, and the last gathering was their removal from Khaybar to the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said that the last gathering is the gathering of all people to the place of assembly, which is the Levant.

ʿIkrimah said: Whoever doubts that the place of assembly on the Day of Resurrection is in the Levant, let him recite this verse. And the Prophet ﷺ said to them, "Leave." They said, "To where?" He said, "To the land of the assembly."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The gathering is first, middle and last. The first is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, the middle is the expulsion of the people of Khaybar, and the last is on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes have agreed that those mentioned in the verse are the Banu al-Nadir. Only al-Hasan al-Basri dissented, saying they were the Banu Qurayza, but this is an error, for the Banu Qurayza were not gathered (expelled) but were killed, by the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh when they agreed to his judgment. He ruled that their fighting men be killed, their children taken captive, and their property seized. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Saʿd, "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above the seven heavens."

The lam in ﴿for the first gathering﴾ (li-awwali al-hashr) is connected to "expelled," and it is the lam of time, like His words: ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ (li-dulūki al-shams) [al-Isra: 78].

﴿You did not think that they would leave.﴾ This is an address to the Muslims: that is, O Muslims, you did not think that the Banu al-Nadir would leave their homes because of their power and their defenses. This was because they were people of strong fortresses, extensive date-palm plantations and estates, and people of numbers and equipment. ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah.﴾ That is, the Banu al-Nadir thought that their fortresses would protect them from the might of Allah. His words "protecting them" (māniʿatuhum) is the predicate placed before its subject, and "their fortresses" (ḥuṣūnuhum) is the delayed subject. The whole clause is the predicate of "that they" (annahum).

It is also permissible that "protecting them" be the predicate of "that they," and "their fortresses" be the agent (fāʿil) of "protecting them." Abu Hayyan preferred the second, but the first is more preferable.

﴿So Allah came at them from where they did not expect.﴾ That is, the command of Allah came upon them from a direction they did not imagine it would come from. This was that He, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to fight them and expel them, and they did not think that would happen.

It was also said that it was the killing of their chief, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and Abu Salih, for his killing weakened their strength.

It was also said that the pronoun in "came at them" and in "they did not expect" refers to the believers: that is, the help of Allah came to them from where they did not expect. But the first is more preferable because of His words: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts,﴾ for the casting of terror was into the hearts of the Banu al-Nadir, not into the hearts of the Muslims.

The people of language said: ruʿb is the fear that terrifies the chest, that is, fills it. Its "casting" (qadhf) is its placing within it.

It was also said that the casting of terror into their hearts was by the killing of their leader Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. But it is better not to restrict it to this or interpret it as such. Rather, what is meant by the terror that Allah cast into their hearts is that which is established in the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) reports from His ﷺ saying: "I have been helped with terror for a distance of a month's journey."

﴿They destroy their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers.﴾ This was because, when they became certain of expulsion, they envied the Muslims that they would live in their dwellings, so they began to ruin them from within, while the Muslims did so from without.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: The believers were demolishing from outside in order to enter, and the Jews were demolishing from inside in order to rebuild what had been ruined of their fortress.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of their destruction by the hands of the believers is that they exposed them to that.

The majority read ﴿yukhribūna﴾ with a single letter (ikhrāb, without the doubling).

al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Abu ʿAmr read it with doubling (tashdīd), as yukharribūna.

Abu ʿAmr said: I chose the doubled reading because ikhrāb means leaving a thing in ruin, whereas they demolished them by razing.

What he said is not accepted, for takhrīb and ikhrāb are, according to the linguists, one and the same in meaning.

Sibawayh said: The meanings of faʿʿala and afʿala (the doubled and the single-letter forms) alternate, as in akhrabtahu and kharrabtahu, and afraḥtahu and farraḥtahu.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose the first reading (the single-letter form).

al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd and ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Prophet ﷺ made peace with them on the condition that they could take whatever the camels could carry, they would take the beams or the pillars and demolish their houses, carrying these on their camels, while the believers would destroy what remained.

al-Zuhri also said: They ruin their houses by breaking the treaty, and the hands of the believers by fighting. Abu ʿAmr said: "by their own hands" refers to their leaving them, and "by the hands of the believers" refers to their expelling them from them. The clause is either a new sentence explaining what they did, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ That is: be admonished, reflect, and consider what befell them, O people of intellect and understanding.

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of iʿtibār (taking warning) is considering matters so that by them something else of the same kind may be known.

﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world.﴾ That is: had it not been that Allah had decreed for them leaving their homelands in that manner and had ordained it for them, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity, as He did to the Banu Qurayza.

Jalaʾ (exile) is leaving one's homeland. One says jalā bi-nafsihi jalāʾan (he left by himself), and ajlāhu ghayruhu ijlāʾan (another made him leave).

The difference between jalāʾ and ikhrāj (expulsion), though their meaning of removal is one in two respects, is: first, that jalāʾ is with family and children, whereas ikhrāj may be with the family and children remaining. Second, jalāʾ occurs only for a group, whereas ikhrāj may be for a group or an individual.

Thus said al-Mawardi.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This sentence is a new statement, not connected to the answer of "had it not been," and it includes an explanation of the punishment they will receive in the Hereafter, even though they escaped the punishment of this world.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the exile in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿Because they opposed Allah and His Messenger.﴾ That is, because of their opposition to Allah and His Messenger, by disobedience, by siding with the disbelievers, and by breaking the covenant. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah - indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ He limited the mention here to opposing Allah, because opposing Him is opposing His Messenger.

The majority read yushāqqi (with doubling). Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read yushāqiqu (without doubling).

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots - it was by permission of Allah.﴾ Mujahid said: Some of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) fell to cutting down the palm trees, and some of them forbade this, saying, "They are only spoils for the Muslims." Those who cut them down said, "Rather, it is a rage for the enemy." So the Qur'an was revealed confirming the one who forbade cutting the palms and lifting the sin from the one who cut them, and said: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down.﴾ Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: They cut down some of their palms and burned six palm trees.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: They cut down one palm tree and burned another. The Banu al-Nadir, who were People of the Book, said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are a prophet who wants righteousness? Is it righteous to cut down palms and burn trees? Did you find in what was revealed to you permission for corruption in the land?" This grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Muslims were troubled within themselves, so the verse was revealed.

The meaning of the verse: whatever you cut down of that or left standing, it was by the permission of Allah. The pronoun in "you left it" refers to "whatever" (mā), by interpreting it as palm trees, and likewise in His words "standing on their roots." The meaning of "on their roots" is that they remained in the state they were in.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of līnah (a type of palm). al-Zuhri, Malik, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and al-Khalil said: it is all palm trees except ʿajwah (a superior variety).

Mujahid said: it is all palm trees, without excepting ʿajwah or anything else.

al-Thawri said: it is the noble palm trees (kirām).

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is all kinds of dates except ʿajwah and barni (other superior varieties).

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: it is only ʿajwah. It was also said: it is a type of palm, whose dates are called al-lawn, and its dates are the finest.

al-Asmaʿi said: it is al-daqal (a low-quality variety). The origin of līnah is lawnah, and the waw was changed to a ya because of the kasra before it. The plural of līnah is līn, and it was also said līyān.

Ibn Masʿud read: "Whatever palm trees you cut down, and you did not leave a people (unpunished)."

﴿On their roots﴾ means standing on their stems. It is also read ʿalā aṣlihā (on its root, singular), and qāʾiman ʿalā uṣūlihi (standing on its roots, with a singular accusative).

﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ That is, that He might humiliate those who go outside obedience, namely the Jews, and enrage them by cutting or leaving them. For when they saw the believers disposing of their property as they wished, cutting or leaving, their rage increased.

al-Zajjaj said: ﴿and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾ by showing them their property being disposed of by the believers as they wished, cutting or leaving. The implied meaning is: and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient, He permitted that. This is indicated by the omitted part, His words ﴿by permission of Allah.﴾ This verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and for holding that the mujtahids (those who exercise ijtihad) are each correct. The discussion is fully treated in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory).

﴿And what Allah returned to His Messenger from them﴾ means what He returned to him of the property of the disbelievers. It is said: fāʾa yafīʾu, meaning he returned. The pronoun in "from them" refers to the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿For you did not urge on it horses or camels.﴾ One says wajafa al-faras wal-baʿīr yajifu wajfan, meaning the horse or camel moved swiftly, and awjafahu ṣāḥibuhu means its rider drove it at a rapid pace. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"Swift and sharp-edged swords, their polish... from the riders, at times, when the riders have pressed on."

And Nuṣayb said:

"Many a caravan have I crossed the rapid journey of, to reach you, and had it not been for you, the caravan would not have pressed on."

The mā in ﴿so you did not urge﴾ is negative, and the fāʾ is the answer to the condition if the mā in His words ﴿what Allah returned﴾ is conditional; if it is relative (mawṣūlah), the fāʾ is extra. The min in ﴿of horses﴾ is extra, for emphasis. The rikāb (riding camels) refers only to camels that are ridden.

The meaning is that what Allah returned to His Messenger of the property of the Banu al-Nadir, you did not ride horses or camels to obtain it, nor did you undertake any journey for it, nor did you encounter in it war or hardship. It was only at two miles from Medina. For this reason Allah, glorified be He, made the property of the Banu al-Nadir exclusively for His Messenger ﷺ.

He took it by treaty and seized its property. The Muslims had asked him to divide it among them, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills.﴾ That is, over His enemies. In this is a clarification that those properties were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not for his companions, because they did not urge horses or camels upon them, but walked to them on foot, and did not endure any of the hardships of fierce wars. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He gives power to whom He wills over whom He wills, gives to whom He wills, and withholds from whom He wills. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾

This is the second part of al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 59, verses 2–7.

﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. This explains the destinations of the fay' (property gained without battle) after the statement that it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specifically. The repetition is for emphasis and affirmation. "The people of the towns" is used in place of "from them", meaning from the Banu al-Nadir, to indicate that this ruling is not restricted to the Banu al-Nadir alone. Rather, it is a ruling applying to every town that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquers by treaty, against which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels.

It has been said that the towns referred to are the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah, Fadak and Khaybar.

The scholars have discussed this verse and the one before it: whether their meanings are the same or different. It has been said that their meanings are the same, as we have mentioned, and it has been said that they differ. On this there is a lengthy discussion among the scholars.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no doubt that they are three meanings in three verses.

As for the first verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from them﴾, it is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is the property of the Banu al-Nadir and what was similar to it.

As for the second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, this is a separate statement, different from the first, with a different entitlement, even though both it and the first share the fact that each of them includes something that Allah restored to His Messenger. The first verse indicates that it was acquired without fighting. The verse of al-Anfal, which is the third verse, indicates that it was acquired by fighting. The second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, is silent about whether it was acquired by fighting or without fighting. From here the disagreement arose. One group said it is attached to the first, and it is the property of the treaty.

Another group said it is attached to the third, which is the verse of al-Anfal.

Those who said it is attached to the verse of al-Anfal disagreed on whether it is abrogated (mansukhah) or unabrogated (muhkamah). This is the substance of his statement.

Malik said: The first verse of this surah is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the second verse concerns the Banu Qurayzah. He means that its meaning returns to the verse of al-Anfal.

The position of al-Shafi'i is that the way of the one-fifth of the fay' is the way of the one-fifth of the ghanimah (spoils of war). Four-fifths of it belonged to the Prophet (ﷺ), and after him it is for the benefit of the Muslims. ﴿So to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveler﴾. The meaning of "to Allah" is that He judges concerning it as He wills. "To the Messenger" means it becomes his possession. "To the near relatives" refers to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because they were prevented from receiving zakat, so a share of the fay' was given to them.

It has been said: The division of this property is such that four-fifths belong to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and its one-fifth is divided into five parts: one part for the Messenger, and one part for each of the four categories mentioned. It has also been said that it is divided into six parts.

The sixth is the share of Allah, the Exalted, and it is spent on the avenues of nearness to Allah, such as the upkeep of mosques and the like. ﴿So that it does not become a circulation among the rich among you﴾. That is, so that the fay' does not become a circulation confined to the rich, excluding the poor. Dawlah is the name for a thing that people pass around among themselves, so that it belongs to this one at one time and to that one at another time.

Muqatil said: The meaning is that the rich overpower the poor and then divide it among themselves.

The majority read yakun with the ya' (third person), and dawlah in the accusative, meaning: so that the fay' does not become a dawlah.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Hisham and Abu Hayyan read it as takun with the ta' (feminine), and dawlah in the nominative, meaning: so that a dawlah does not occur or come into being; here kana is used as a complete verb.

The majority read dawlah with a damma on the dal.

Abu Haywah and al-Sulami read it with a fatha on the dal.

'Isa ibn 'Umar, Yunus and al-Asma'i said: They are two dialects with one meaning.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: Dawlah with a fatha is that which is passed around among the property, and with a damma it is the action.

Abu 'Ubaydah also said the same.

Then, when He, the Exalted, had explained to them the destinations of this property, He commanded them to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. That is: whatever he gives you from the property of spoils, take it, and whatever he forbids you from taking, refrain from it and do not take it.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: Whatever he gives you from the property of the fay', accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it.

Ibn Juraij said: Whatever he brings you of obedience to Me, do it, and whatever he forbids you of disobedience to Me, avoid it.

The truth is that this verse is general to everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brings, whether a command, a prohibition, a saying or an action.

And even if the occasion of revelation is specific, what is taken into account is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Everything that he has brought to us of the Shari'ah, he has given to us and conveyed to us.

How beneficial this verse is, and how great its benefit is.

Then, when He had commanded them to take what the Messenger commanded them and to leave what he forbade them, He commanded them to be mindful of Him and warned them of the severity of His punishment.

He said: ﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾. So He punishes whoever does not take what the Messenger brought and does not refrain from what he forbade.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The expedition of the Banu al-Nadir, who were a group of the Jews, took place six months after the Battle of Badr. Their dwelling and their palm trees were in the outskirts of Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged them until they agreed to depart, and on condition that they could take with them whatever the camels could carry of goods and property, except the hilqah, meaning weapons. So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿For the first gathering. You did not think that they would leave﴾. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) fought them until they made peace with him on the condition of exile, and he sent them to Syria. They were from a tribe that had not previously been exiled, and Allah had decreed this upon them. Had it not been for that, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity.

As for His saying, ﴿for the first gathering﴾, their exile was the first gathering in this world, to Syria.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: Whoever doubts that the place of gathering is in Syria, let him recite this verse: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them on that day: Depart! They said: To where? He said: To the land of the gathering.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had besieged them until he had inflicted on them every kind of hardship. So they gave him what he wanted from them, and he made peace with them on the condition that he would spare their lives, that he would expel them from their land and homelands, and that they would travel to Adhri'at in Syria. He gave each three of them one camel and one water-skin.

In al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned and cut down the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir, and it was at al-Buwayrah, and Hassan said concerning it:

"It was humiliating to the nobles of the Banu Lu'ayy
A burning at al-Buwayrah, spreading far."

Then Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse: He said: Al-linah is the palm tree. ﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾. He said: They forced them down from their fortresses and ordered the cutting of the palm trees, and this stirred something in their hearts. The Muslims said: We have cut down some and left some, so let us ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Is there a reward for us in what we cut down, and is there a sin upon us for what we left? So Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, the verse. There are also other hadiths on this subject. The account of the treaty with the Banu al-Nadir is expounded in the books of biography (sirah).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah restored to His Messenger, from which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels, and it was specifically for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He used to spend from it on his family the provision of a year, and then he would place what remained in weapons and horses as preparation for the cause of Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿You did not advance against it with horses or camels﴾: So what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acquired, he would judge concerning it as he wished, and there were no horses or camels on that day that could be advanced with.

He said: The ijafah (advancing) is pressing the pace. And it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). From that were Khaybar, Fadak and the villages of 'Uraynah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to head for Yanbu', and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went there and took possession of all of it. Some people said: Why did Allah not divide it? So Allah revealed His excuse, saying: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: What Allah restored to His Messenger from Khaybar was half for Allah and His Messenger, and the other half for the Muslims. What belonged to Allah and His Messenger from it were al-Kathibah, al-Wati', Salalim and Wajrah. What belonged to the Muslims was the Shiqq, and the Shiqq was thirteen shares, and Natah was five shares. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not divide anything from Khaybar among the Muslims except for those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not permit any of the Muslims who had stayed behind from him when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah to attend Khaybar with him, except Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari.

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had choice property (safaya) from al-Nadir, Khaybar and Fadak. As for the Banu al-Nadir, it was held in reserve for his emergencies. As for Fadak, it was for the wayfarer. As for Khaybar, he divided it into three parts: he distributed two parts among the Muslims, and he kept one part for himself and for the provision of his family. Whatever remained beyond his family's provision, he returned to the poor among the Muhajirun.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Zanjawayh in al-Amwal, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: There is no Muslim on the face of the earth except that he has a right in this fay', except what your right hands possess.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and the women who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair, and the women who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah. This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub. She came to Ibn Mas'ud and said: It has reached me that you have cursed so-and-so and so-and-so. He said: And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah? She said: I have read what is between the two covers (of the Qur'an) and I did not find anything of this in it. He said: If you had read it, you would have found it. Did you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾? She said: Yes. He said: Then he has forbidden it.

[p. 1475]

Its revelation place is Medinan.

Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Surat al-Hashr was revealed in Medina.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas, "Surat al-Hashr?" He said, "Surat al-Nadir." He meant that it was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir, as he stated explicitly in some narrations.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The exegesis of this has already been given in Surat al-Hadid.

﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering.﴾ They are the Banu al-Nadir, a group of Jews of the descendants of Harun (Aaron). They settled in Medina during the trials of the Children of Israel, expecting Muhammad ﷺ. They betrayed the Prophet ﷺ after they had made a covenant with him, and sided with the polytheists against him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ besieged them until they agreed to leave.

al-Kalbi said: They were the first of the protected people (dhimmis, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection) to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula. Then the last of them were expelled in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. Their expulsion was thus the first gathering from Medina, and ʿUmar's expulsion of them was the last gathering.

It was also said that the first gathering was their removal from their fortresses to Khaybar, and the last gathering was their removal from Khaybar to the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said that the last gathering is the gathering of all people to the place of assembly, which is the Levant.

ʿIkrimah said: Whoever doubts that the place of assembly on the Day of Resurrection is in the Levant, let him recite this verse. And the Prophet ﷺ said to them, "Leave." They said, "To where?" He said, "To the land of the assembly."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The gathering is first, middle and last. The first is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, the middle is the expulsion of the people of Khaybar, and the last is on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes have agreed that those mentioned in the verse are the Banu al-Nadir. Only al-Hasan al-Basri dissented, saying they were the Banu Qurayza, but this is an error, for the Banu Qurayza were not gathered (expelled) but were killed, by the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh when they agreed to his judgment. He ruled that their fighting men be killed, their children taken captive, and their property seized. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Saʿd, "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above the seven heavens."

The lam in ﴿for the first gathering﴾ (li-awwali al-hashr) is connected to "expelled," and it is the lam of time, like His words: ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ (li-dulūki al-shams) [al-Isra: 78].

﴿You did not think that they would leave.﴾ This is an address to the Muslims: that is, O Muslims, you did not think that the Banu al-Nadir would leave their homes because of their power and their defenses. This was because they were people of strong fortresses, extensive date-palm plantations and estates, and people of numbers and equipment. ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah.﴾ That is, the Banu al-Nadir thought that their fortresses would protect them from the might of Allah. His words "protecting them" (māniʿatuhum) is the predicate placed before its subject, and "their fortresses" (ḥuṣūnuhum) is the delayed subject. The whole clause is the predicate of "that they" (annahum).

It is also permissible that "protecting them" be the predicate of "that they," and "their fortresses" be the agent (fāʿil) of "protecting them." Abu Hayyan preferred the second, but the first is more preferable.

﴿So Allah came at them from where they did not expect.﴾ That is, the command of Allah came upon them from a direction they did not imagine it would come from. This was that He, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to fight them and expel them, and they did not think that would happen.

It was also said that it was the killing of their chief, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and Abu Salih, for his killing weakened their strength.

It was also said that the pronoun in "came at them" and in "they did not expect" refers to the believers: that is, the help of Allah came to them from where they did not expect. But the first is more preferable because of His words: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts,﴾ for the casting of terror was into the hearts of the Banu al-Nadir, not into the hearts of the Muslims.

The people of language said: ruʿb is the fear that terrifies the chest, that is, fills it. Its "casting" (qadhf) is its placing within it.

It was also said that the casting of terror into their hearts was by the killing of their leader Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. But it is better not to restrict it to this or interpret it as such. Rather, what is meant by the terror that Allah cast into their hearts is that which is established in the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) reports from His ﷺ saying: "I have been helped with terror for a distance of a month's journey."

﴿They destroy their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers.﴾ This was because, when they became certain of expulsion, they envied the Muslims that they would live in their dwellings, so they began to ruin them from within, while the Muslims did so from without.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: The believers were demolishing from outside in order to enter, and the Jews were demolishing from inside in order to rebuild what had been ruined of their fortress.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of their destruction by the hands of the believers is that they exposed them to that.

The majority read ﴿yukhribūna﴾ with a single letter (ikhrāb, without the doubling).

al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Abu ʿAmr read it with doubling (tashdīd), as yukharribūna.

Abu ʿAmr said: I chose the doubled reading because ikhrāb means leaving a thing in ruin, whereas they demolished them by razing.

What he said is not accepted, for takhrīb and ikhrāb are, according to the linguists, one and the same in meaning.

Sibawayh said: The meanings of faʿʿala and afʿala (the doubled and the single-letter forms) alternate, as in akhrabtahu and kharrabtahu, and afraḥtahu and farraḥtahu.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose the first reading (the single-letter form).

al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd and ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Prophet ﷺ made peace with them on the condition that they could take whatever the camels could carry, they would take the beams or the pillars and demolish their houses, carrying these on their camels, while the believers would destroy what remained.

al-Zuhri also said: They ruin their houses by breaking the treaty, and the hands of the believers by fighting. Abu ʿAmr said: "by their own hands" refers to their leaving them, and "by the hands of the believers" refers to their expelling them from them. The clause is either a new sentence explaining what they did, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ That is: be admonished, reflect, and consider what befell them, O people of intellect and understanding.

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of iʿtibār (taking warning) is considering matters so that by them something else of the same kind may be known.

﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world.﴾ That is: had it not been that Allah had decreed for them leaving their homelands in that manner and had ordained it for them, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity, as He did to the Banu Qurayza.

Jalaʾ (exile) is leaving one's homeland. One says jalā bi-nafsihi jalāʾan (he left by himself), and ajlāhu ghayruhu ijlāʾan (another made him leave).

The difference between jalāʾ and ikhrāj (expulsion), though their meaning of removal is one in two respects, is: first, that jalāʾ is with family and children, whereas ikhrāj may be with the family and children remaining. Second, jalāʾ occurs only for a group, whereas ikhrāj may be for a group or an individual.

Thus said al-Mawardi.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This sentence is a new statement, not connected to the answer of "had it not been," and it includes an explanation of the punishment they will receive in the Hereafter, even though they escaped the punishment of this world.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the exile in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿Because they opposed Allah and His Messenger.﴾ That is, because of their opposition to Allah and His Messenger, by disobedience, by siding with the disbelievers, and by breaking the covenant. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah - indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ He limited the mention here to opposing Allah, because opposing Him is opposing His Messenger.

The majority read yushāqqi (with doubling). Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read yushāqiqu (without doubling).

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots - it was by permission of Allah.﴾ Mujahid said: Some of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) fell to cutting down the palm trees, and some of them forbade this, saying, "They are only spoils for the Muslims." Those who cut them down said, "Rather, it is a rage for the enemy." So the Qur'an was revealed confirming the one who forbade cutting the palms and lifting the sin from the one who cut them, and said: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down.﴾ Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: They cut down some of their palms and burned six palm trees.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: They cut down one palm tree and burned another. The Banu al-Nadir, who were People of the Book, said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are a prophet who wants righteousness? Is it righteous to cut down palms and burn trees? Did you find in what was revealed to you permission for corruption in the land?" This grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Muslims were troubled within themselves, so the verse was revealed.

The meaning of the verse: whatever you cut down of that or left standing, it was by the permission of Allah. The pronoun in "you left it" refers to "whatever" (mā), by interpreting it as palm trees, and likewise in His words "standing on their roots." The meaning of "on their roots" is that they remained in the state they were in.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of līnah (a type of palm). al-Zuhri, Malik, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and al-Khalil said: it is all palm trees except ʿajwah (a superior variety).

Mujahid said: it is all palm trees, without excepting ʿajwah or anything else.

al-Thawri said: it is the noble palm trees (kirām).

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is all kinds of dates except ʿajwah and barni (other superior varieties).

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: it is only ʿajwah. It was also said: it is a type of palm, whose dates are called al-lawn, and its dates are the finest.

al-Asmaʿi said: it is al-daqal (a low-quality variety). The origin of līnah is lawnah, and the waw was changed to a ya because of the kasra before it. The plural of līnah is līn, and it was also said līyān.

Ibn Masʿud read: "Whatever palm trees you cut down, and you did not leave a people (unpunished)."

﴿On their roots﴾ means standing on their stems. It is also read ʿalā aṣlihā (on its root, singular), and qāʾiman ʿalā uṣūlihi (standing on its roots, with a singular accusative).

﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ That is, that He might humiliate those who go outside obedience, namely the Jews, and enrage them by cutting or leaving them. For when they saw the believers disposing of their property as they wished, cutting or leaving, their rage increased.

al-Zajjaj said: ﴿and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾ by showing them their property being disposed of by the believers as they wished, cutting or leaving. The implied meaning is: and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient, He permitted that. This is indicated by the omitted part, His words ﴿by permission of Allah.﴾ This verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and for holding that the mujtahids (those who exercise ijtihad) are each correct. The discussion is fully treated in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory).

﴿And what Allah returned to His Messenger from them﴾ means what He returned to him of the property of the disbelievers. It is said: fāʾa yafīʾu, meaning he returned. The pronoun in "from them" refers to the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿For you did not urge on it horses or camels.﴾ One says wajafa al-faras wal-baʿīr yajifu wajfan, meaning the horse or camel moved swiftly, and awjafahu ṣāḥibuhu means its rider drove it at a rapid pace. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"Swift and sharp-edged swords, their polish... from the riders, at times, when the riders have pressed on."

And Nuṣayb said:

"Many a caravan have I crossed the rapid journey of, to reach you, and had it not been for you, the caravan would not have pressed on."

The mā in ﴿so you did not urge﴾ is negative, and the fāʾ is the answer to the condition if the mā in His words ﴿what Allah returned﴾ is conditional; if it is relative (mawṣūlah), the fāʾ is extra. The min in ﴿of horses﴾ is extra, for emphasis. The rikāb (riding camels) refers only to camels that are ridden.

The meaning is that what Allah returned to His Messenger of the property of the Banu al-Nadir, you did not ride horses or camels to obtain it, nor did you undertake any journey for it, nor did you encounter in it war or hardship. It was only at two miles from Medina. For this reason Allah, glorified be He, made the property of the Banu al-Nadir exclusively for His Messenger ﷺ.

He took it by treaty and seized its property. The Muslims had asked him to divide it among them, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills.﴾ That is, over His enemies. In this is a clarification that those properties were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not for his companions, because they did not urge horses or camels upon them, but walked to them on foot, and did not endure any of the hardships of fierce wars. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He gives power to whom He wills over whom He wills, gives to whom He wills, and withholds from whom He wills. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾

This is the second part of al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 59, verses 2–7.

﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. This explains the destinations of the fay' (property gained without battle) after the statement that it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specifically. The repetition is for emphasis and affirmation. "The people of the towns" is used in place of "from them", meaning from the Banu al-Nadir, to indicate that this ruling is not restricted to the Banu al-Nadir alone. Rather, it is a ruling applying to every town that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquers by treaty, against which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels.

It has been said that the towns referred to are the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah, Fadak and Khaybar.

The scholars have discussed this verse and the one before it: whether their meanings are the same or different. It has been said that their meanings are the same, as we have mentioned, and it has been said that they differ. On this there is a lengthy discussion among the scholars.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no doubt that they are three meanings in three verses.

As for the first verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from them﴾, it is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is the property of the Banu al-Nadir and what was similar to it.

As for the second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, this is a separate statement, different from the first, with a different entitlement, even though both it and the first share the fact that each of them includes something that Allah restored to His Messenger. The first verse indicates that it was acquired without fighting. The verse of al-Anfal, which is the third verse, indicates that it was acquired by fighting. The second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, is silent about whether it was acquired by fighting or without fighting. From here the disagreement arose. One group said it is attached to the first, and it is the property of the treaty.

Another group said it is attached to the third, which is the verse of al-Anfal.

Those who said it is attached to the verse of al-Anfal disagreed on whether it is abrogated (mansukhah) or unabrogated (muhkamah). This is the substance of his statement.

Malik said: The first verse of this surah is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the second verse concerns the Banu Qurayzah. He means that its meaning returns to the verse of al-Anfal.

The position of al-Shafi'i is that the way of the one-fifth of the fay' is the way of the one-fifth of the ghanimah (spoils of war). Four-fifths of it belonged to the Prophet (ﷺ), and after him it is for the benefit of the Muslims. ﴿So to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveler﴾. The meaning of "to Allah" is that He judges concerning it as He wills. "To the Messenger" means it becomes his possession. "To the near relatives" refers to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because they were prevented from receiving zakat, so a share of the fay' was given to them.

It has been said: The division of this property is such that four-fifths belong to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and its one-fifth is divided into five parts: one part for the Messenger, and one part for each of the four categories mentioned. It has also been said that it is divided into six parts.

The sixth is the share of Allah, the Exalted, and it is spent on the avenues of nearness to Allah, such as the upkeep of mosques and the like. ﴿So that it does not become a circulation among the rich among you﴾. That is, so that the fay' does not become a circulation confined to the rich, excluding the poor. Dawlah is the name for a thing that people pass around among themselves, so that it belongs to this one at one time and to that one at another time.

Muqatil said: The meaning is that the rich overpower the poor and then divide it among themselves.

The majority read yakun with the ya' (third person), and dawlah in the accusative, meaning: so that the fay' does not become a dawlah.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Hisham and Abu Hayyan read it as takun with the ta' (feminine), and dawlah in the nominative, meaning: so that a dawlah does not occur or come into being; here kana is used as a complete verb.

The majority read dawlah with a damma on the dal.

Abu Haywah and al-Sulami read it with a fatha on the dal.

'Isa ibn 'Umar, Yunus and al-Asma'i said: They are two dialects with one meaning.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: Dawlah with a fatha is that which is passed around among the property, and with a damma it is the action.

Abu 'Ubaydah also said the same.

Then, when He, the Exalted, had explained to them the destinations of this property, He commanded them to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. That is: whatever he gives you from the property of spoils, take it, and whatever he forbids you from taking, refrain from it and do not take it.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: Whatever he gives you from the property of the fay', accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it.

Ibn Juraij said: Whatever he brings you of obedience to Me, do it, and whatever he forbids you of disobedience to Me, avoid it.

The truth is that this verse is general to everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brings, whether a command, a prohibition, a saying or an action.

And even if the occasion of revelation is specific, what is taken into account is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Everything that he has brought to us of the Shari'ah, he has given to us and conveyed to us.

How beneficial this verse is, and how great its benefit is.

Then, when He had commanded them to take what the Messenger commanded them and to leave what he forbade them, He commanded them to be mindful of Him and warned them of the severity of His punishment.

He said: ﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾. So He punishes whoever does not take what the Messenger brought and does not refrain from what he forbade.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The expedition of the Banu al-Nadir, who were a group of the Jews, took place six months after the Battle of Badr. Their dwelling and their palm trees were in the outskirts of Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged them until they agreed to depart, and on condition that they could take with them whatever the camels could carry of goods and property, except the hilqah, meaning weapons. So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿For the first gathering. You did not think that they would leave﴾. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) fought them until they made peace with him on the condition of exile, and he sent them to Syria. They were from a tribe that had not previously been exiled, and Allah had decreed this upon them. Had it not been for that, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity.

As for His saying, ﴿for the first gathering﴾, their exile was the first gathering in this world, to Syria.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: Whoever doubts that the place of gathering is in Syria, let him recite this verse: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them on that day: Depart! They said: To where? He said: To the land of the gathering.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had besieged them until he had inflicted on them every kind of hardship. So they gave him what he wanted from them, and he made peace with them on the condition that he would spare their lives, that he would expel them from their land and homelands, and that they would travel to Adhri'at in Syria. He gave each three of them one camel and one water-skin.

In al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned and cut down the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir, and it was at al-Buwayrah, and Hassan said concerning it:

"It was humiliating to the nobles of the Banu Lu'ayy
A burning at al-Buwayrah, spreading far."

Then Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse: He said: Al-linah is the palm tree. ﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾. He said: They forced them down from their fortresses and ordered the cutting of the palm trees, and this stirred something in their hearts. The Muslims said: We have cut down some and left some, so let us ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Is there a reward for us in what we cut down, and is there a sin upon us for what we left? So Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, the verse. There are also other hadiths on this subject. The account of the treaty with the Banu al-Nadir is expounded in the books of biography (sirah).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah restored to His Messenger, from which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels, and it was specifically for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He used to spend from it on his family the provision of a year, and then he would place what remained in weapons and horses as preparation for the cause of Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿You did not advance against it with horses or camels﴾: So what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acquired, he would judge concerning it as he wished, and there were no horses or camels on that day that could be advanced with.

He said: The ijafah (advancing) is pressing the pace. And it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). From that were Khaybar, Fadak and the villages of 'Uraynah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to head for Yanbu', and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went there and took possession of all of it. Some people said: Why did Allah not divide it? So Allah revealed His excuse, saying: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: What Allah restored to His Messenger from Khaybar was half for Allah and His Messenger, and the other half for the Muslims. What belonged to Allah and His Messenger from it were al-Kathibah, al-Wati', Salalim and Wajrah. What belonged to the Muslims was the Shiqq, and the Shiqq was thirteen shares, and Natah was five shares. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not divide anything from Khaybar among the Muslims except for those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not permit any of the Muslims who had stayed behind from him when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah to attend Khaybar with him, except Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari.

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had choice property (safaya) from al-Nadir, Khaybar and Fadak. As for the Banu al-Nadir, it was held in reserve for his emergencies. As for Fadak, it was for the wayfarer. As for Khaybar, he divided it into three parts: he distributed two parts among the Muslims, and he kept one part for himself and for the provision of his family. Whatever remained beyond his family's provision, he returned to the poor among the Muhajirun.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Zanjawayh in al-Amwal, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: There is no Muslim on the face of the earth except that he has a right in this fay', except what your right hands possess.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and the women who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair, and the women who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah. This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub. She came to Ibn Mas'ud and said: It has reached me that you have cursed so-and-so and so-and-so. He said: And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah? She said: I have read what is between the two covers (of the Qur'an) and I did not find anything of this in it. He said: If you had read it, you would have found it. Did you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾? She said: Yes. He said: Then he has forbidden it.

[p. 1475]

Its revelation place is Medinan.

Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Surat al-Hashr was revealed in Medina.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas, "Surat al-Hashr?" He said, "Surat al-Nadir." He meant that it was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir, as he stated explicitly in some narrations.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The exegesis of this has already been given in Surat al-Hadid.

﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering.﴾ They are the Banu al-Nadir, a group of Jews of the descendants of Harun (Aaron). They settled in Medina during the trials of the Children of Israel, expecting Muhammad ﷺ. They betrayed the Prophet ﷺ after they had made a covenant with him, and sided with the polytheists against him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ besieged them until they agreed to leave.

al-Kalbi said: They were the first of the protected people (dhimmis, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection) to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula. Then the last of them were expelled in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. Their expulsion was thus the first gathering from Medina, and ʿUmar's expulsion of them was the last gathering.

It was also said that the first gathering was their removal from their fortresses to Khaybar, and the last gathering was their removal from Khaybar to the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said that the last gathering is the gathering of all people to the place of assembly, which is the Levant.

ʿIkrimah said: Whoever doubts that the place of assembly on the Day of Resurrection is in the Levant, let him recite this verse. And the Prophet ﷺ said to them, "Leave." They said, "To where?" He said, "To the land of the assembly."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The gathering is first, middle and last. The first is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, the middle is the expulsion of the people of Khaybar, and the last is on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes have agreed that those mentioned in the verse are the Banu al-Nadir. Only al-Hasan al-Basri dissented, saying they were the Banu Qurayza, but this is an error, for the Banu Qurayza were not gathered (expelled) but were killed, by the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh when they agreed to his judgment. He ruled that their fighting men be killed, their children taken captive, and their property seized. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Saʿd, "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above the seven heavens."

The lam in ﴿for the first gathering﴾ (li-awwali al-hashr) is connected to "expelled," and it is the lam of time, like His words: ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ (li-dulūki al-shams) [al-Isra: 78].

﴿You did not think that they would leave.﴾ This is an address to the Muslims: that is, O Muslims, you did not think that the Banu al-Nadir would leave their homes because of their power and their defenses. This was because they were people of strong fortresses, extensive date-palm plantations and estates, and people of numbers and equipment. ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah.﴾ That is, the Banu al-Nadir thought that their fortresses would protect them from the might of Allah. His words "protecting them" (māniʿatuhum) is the predicate placed before its subject, and "their fortresses" (ḥuṣūnuhum) is the delayed subject. The whole clause is the predicate of "that they" (annahum).

It is also permissible that "protecting them" be the predicate of "that they," and "their fortresses" be the agent (fāʿil) of "protecting them." Abu Hayyan preferred the second, but the first is more preferable.

﴿So Allah came at them from where they did not expect.﴾ That is, the command of Allah came upon them from a direction they did not imagine it would come from. This was that He, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to fight them and expel them, and they did not think that would happen.

It was also said that it was the killing of their chief, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and Abu Salih, for his killing weakened their strength.

It was also said that the pronoun in "came at them" and in "they did not expect" refers to the believers: that is, the help of Allah came to them from where they did not expect. But the first is more preferable because of His words: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts,﴾ for the casting of terror was into the hearts of the Banu al-Nadir, not into the hearts of the Muslims.

The people of language said: ruʿb is the fear that terrifies the chest, that is, fills it. Its "casting" (qadhf) is its placing within it.

It was also said that the casting of terror into their hearts was by the killing of their leader Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. But it is better not to restrict it to this or interpret it as such. Rather, what is meant by the terror that Allah cast into their hearts is that which is established in the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) reports from His ﷺ saying: "I have been helped with terror for a distance of a month's journey."

﴿They destroy their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers.﴾ This was because, when they became certain of expulsion, they envied the Muslims that they would live in their dwellings, so they began to ruin them from within, while the Muslims did so from without.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: The believers were demolishing from outside in order to enter, and the Jews were demolishing from inside in order to rebuild what had been ruined of their fortress.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of their destruction by the hands of the believers is that they exposed them to that.

The majority read ﴿yukhribūna﴾ with a single letter (ikhrāb, without the doubling).

al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Abu ʿAmr read it with doubling (tashdīd), as yukharribūna.

Abu ʿAmr said: I chose the doubled reading because ikhrāb means leaving a thing in ruin, whereas they demolished them by razing.

What he said is not accepted, for takhrīb and ikhrāb are, according to the linguists, one and the same in meaning.

Sibawayh said: The meanings of faʿʿala and afʿala (the doubled and the single-letter forms) alternate, as in akhrabtahu and kharrabtahu, and afraḥtahu and farraḥtahu.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose the first reading (the single-letter form).

al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd and ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Prophet ﷺ made peace with them on the condition that they could take whatever the camels could carry, they would take the beams or the pillars and demolish their houses, carrying these on their camels, while the believers would destroy what remained.

al-Zuhri also said: They ruin their houses by breaking the treaty, and the hands of the believers by fighting. Abu ʿAmr said: "by their own hands" refers to their leaving them, and "by the hands of the believers" refers to their expelling them from them. The clause is either a new sentence explaining what they did, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ That is: be admonished, reflect, and consider what befell them, O people of intellect and understanding.

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of iʿtibār (taking warning) is considering matters so that by them something else of the same kind may be known.

﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world.﴾ That is: had it not been that Allah had decreed for them leaving their homelands in that manner and had ordained it for them, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity, as He did to the Banu Qurayza.

Jalaʾ (exile) is leaving one's homeland. One says jalā bi-nafsihi jalāʾan (he left by himself), and ajlāhu ghayruhu ijlāʾan (another made him leave).

The difference between jalāʾ and ikhrāj (expulsion), though their meaning of removal is one in two respects, is: first, that jalāʾ is with family and children, whereas ikhrāj may be with the family and children remaining. Second, jalāʾ occurs only for a group, whereas ikhrāj may be for a group or an individual.

Thus said al-Mawardi.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This sentence is a new statement, not connected to the answer of "had it not been," and it includes an explanation of the punishment they will receive in the Hereafter, even though they escaped the punishment of this world.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the exile in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿Because they opposed Allah and His Messenger.﴾ That is, because of their opposition to Allah and His Messenger, by disobedience, by siding with the disbelievers, and by breaking the covenant. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah - indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ He limited the mention here to opposing Allah, because opposing Him is opposing His Messenger.

The majority read yushāqqi (with doubling). Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read yushāqiqu (without doubling).

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots - it was by permission of Allah.﴾ Mujahid said: Some of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) fell to cutting down the palm trees, and some of them forbade this, saying, "They are only spoils for the Muslims." Those who cut them down said, "Rather, it is a rage for the enemy." So the Qur'an was revealed confirming the one who forbade cutting the palms and lifting the sin from the one who cut them, and said: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down.﴾ Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: They cut down some of their palms and burned six palm trees.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: They cut down one palm tree and burned another. The Banu al-Nadir, who were People of the Book, said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are a prophet who wants righteousness? Is it righteous to cut down palms and burn trees? Did you find in what was revealed to you permission for corruption in the land?" This grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Muslims were troubled within themselves, so the verse was revealed.

The meaning of the verse: whatever you cut down of that or left standing, it was by the permission of Allah. The pronoun in "you left it" refers to "whatever" (mā), by interpreting it as palm trees, and likewise in His words "standing on their roots." The meaning of "on their roots" is that they remained in the state they were in.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of līnah (a type of palm). al-Zuhri, Malik, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and al-Khalil said: it is all palm trees except ʿajwah (a superior variety).

Mujahid said: it is all palm trees, without excepting ʿajwah or anything else.

al-Thawri said: it is the noble palm trees (kirām).

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is all kinds of dates except ʿajwah and barni (other superior varieties).

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: it is only ʿajwah. It was also said: it is a type of palm, whose dates are called al-lawn, and its dates are the finest.

al-Asmaʿi said: it is al-daqal (a low-quality variety). The origin of līnah is lawnah, and the waw was changed to a ya because of the kasra before it. The plural of līnah is līn, and it was also said līyān.

Ibn Masʿud read: "Whatever palm trees you cut down, and you did not leave a people (unpunished)."

﴿On their roots﴾ means standing on their stems. It is also read ʿalā aṣlihā (on its root, singular), and qāʾiman ʿalā uṣūlihi (standing on its roots, with a singular accusative).

﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ That is, that He might humiliate those who go outside obedience, namely the Jews, and enrage them by cutting or leaving them. For when they saw the believers disposing of their property as they wished, cutting or leaving, their rage increased.

al-Zajjaj said: ﴿and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾ by showing them their property being disposed of by the believers as they wished, cutting or leaving. The implied meaning is: and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient, He permitted that.
