The difference between jalāʾ and ikhrāj (expulsion), though their meaning of removal is one in two respects, is: first, that jalāʾ is with family and children, whereas ikhrāj may be with the family and children remaining. Second, jalāʾ occurs only for a group, whereas ikhrāj may be for a group or an individual.

Thus said al-Mawardi.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This sentence is a new statement, not connected to the answer of "had it not been," and it includes an explanation of the punishment they will receive in the Hereafter, even though they escaped the punishment of this world.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the exile in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿Because they opposed Allah and His Messenger.﴾ That is, because of their opposition to Allah and His Messenger, by disobedience, by siding with the disbelievers, and by breaking the covenant. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah - indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ He limited the mention here to opposing Allah, because opposing Him is opposing His Messenger.

The majority read yushāqqi (with doubling). Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read yushāqiqu (without doubling).

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots - it was by permission of Allah.﴾ Mujahid said: Some of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) fell to cutting down the palm trees, and some of them forbade this, saying, "They are only spoils for the Muslims." Those who cut them down said, "Rather, it is a rage for the enemy." So the Qur'an was revealed confirming the one who forbade cutting the palms and lifting the sin from the one who cut them, and said: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down.﴾ Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: They cut down some of their palms and burned six palm trees.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: They cut down one palm tree and burned another. The Banu al-Nadir, who were People of the Book, said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are a prophet who wants righteousness? Is it righteous to cut down palms and burn trees? Did you find in what was revealed to you permission for corruption in the land?" This grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Muslims were troubled within themselves, so the verse was revealed.

The meaning of the verse: whatever you cut down of that or left standing, it was by the permission of Allah. The pronoun in "you left it" refers to "whatever" (mā), by interpreting it as palm trees, and likewise in His words "standing on their roots." The meaning of "on their roots" is that they remained in the state they were in.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of līnah (a type of palm). al-Zuhri, Malik, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and al-Khalil said: it is all palm trees except ʿajwah (a superior variety).

Mujahid said: it is all palm trees, without excepting ʿajwah or anything else.

al-Thawri said: it is the noble palm trees (kirām).

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is all kinds of dates except ʿajwah and barni (other superior varieties).

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: it is only ʿajwah. It was also said: it is a type of palm, whose dates are called al-lawn, and its dates are the finest.

al-Asmaʿi said: it is al-daqal (a low-quality variety). The origin of līnah is lawnah, and the waw was changed to a ya because of the kasra before it. The plural of līnah is līn, and it was also said līyān.

Ibn Masʿud read: "Whatever palm trees you cut down, and you did not leave a people (unpunished)."

﴿On their roots﴾ means standing on their stems. It is also read ʿalā aṣlihā (on its root, singular), and qāʾiman ʿalā uṣūlihi (standing on its roots, with a singular accusative).

﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ That is, that He might humiliate those who go outside obedience, namely the Jews, and enrage them by cutting or leaving them. For when they saw the believers disposing of their property as they wished, cutting or leaving, their rage increased.

al-Zajjaj said: ﴿and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾ by showing them their property being disposed of by the believers as they wished, cutting or leaving. The implied meaning is: and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient, He permitted that. This is indicated by the omitted part, His words ﴿by permission of Allah.﴾ This verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and for holding that the mujtahids (those who exercise ijtihad) are each correct. The discussion is fully treated in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory).

﴿And what Allah returned to His Messenger from them﴾ means what He returned to him of the property of the disbelievers. It is said: fāʾa yafīʾu, meaning he returned. The pronoun in "from them" refers to the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿For you did not urge on it horses or camels.﴾ One says wajafa al-faras wal-baʿīr yajifu wajfan, meaning the horse or camel moved swiftly, and awjafahu ṣāḥibuhu means its rider drove it at a rapid pace. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"Swift and sharp-edged swords, their polish... from the riders, at times, when the riders have pressed on."

And Nuṣayb said:

"Many a caravan have I crossed the rapid journey of, to reach you, and had it not been for you, the caravan would not have pressed on."

The mā in ﴿so you did not urge﴾ is negative, and the fāʾ is the answer to the condition if the mā in His words ﴿what Allah returned﴾ is conditional; if it is relative (mawṣūlah), the fāʾ is extra. The min in ﴿of horses﴾ is extra, for emphasis. The rikāb (riding camels) refers only to camels that are ridden.

The meaning is that what Allah returned to His Messenger of the property of the Banu al-Nadir, you did not ride horses or camels to obtain it, nor did you undertake any journey for it, nor did you encounter in it war or hardship. It was only at two miles from Medina. For this reason Allah, glorified be He, made the property of the Banu al-Nadir exclusively for His Messenger ﷺ.

He took it by treaty and seized its property. The Muslims had asked him to divide it among them, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills.﴾ That is, over His enemies. In this is a clarification that those properties were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not for his companions, because they did not urge horses or camels upon them, but walked to them on foot, and did not endure any of the hardships of fierce wars. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He gives power to whom He wills over whom He wills, gives to whom He wills, and withholds from whom He wills. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾

This is the second part of al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 59, verses 2–7.

﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. This explains the destinations of the fay' (property gained without battle) after the statement that it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specifically. The repetition is for emphasis and affirmation. "The people of the towns" is used in place of "from them", meaning from the Banu al-Nadir, to indicate that this ruling is not restricted to the Banu al-Nadir alone. Rather, it is a ruling applying to every town that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquers by treaty, against which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels.

It has been said that the towns referred to are the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah, Fadak and Khaybar.

The scholars have discussed this verse and the one before it: whether their meanings are the same or different. It has been said that their meanings are the same, as we have mentioned, and it has been said that they differ. On this there is a lengthy discussion among the scholars.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no doubt that they are three meanings in three verses.

As for the first verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from them﴾, it is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is the property of the Banu al-Nadir and what was similar to it.

As for the second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, this is a separate statement, different from the first, with a different entitlement, even though both it and the first share the fact that each of them includes something that Allah restored to His Messenger. The first verse indicates that it was acquired without fighting. The verse of al-Anfal, which is the third verse, indicates that it was acquired by fighting. The second verse, which is His saying, ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, is silent about whether it was acquired by fighting or without fighting. From here the disagreement arose. One group said it is attached to the first, and it is the property of the treaty.

Another group said it is attached to the third, which is the verse of al-Anfal.

Those who said it is attached to the verse of al-Anfal disagreed on whether it is abrogated (mansukhah) or unabrogated (muhkamah). This is the substance of his statement.

Malik said: The first verse of this surah is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the second verse concerns the Banu Qurayzah. He means that its meaning returns to the verse of al-Anfal.

The position of al-Shafi'i is that the way of the one-fifth of the fay' is the way of the one-fifth of the ghanimah (spoils of war). Four-fifths of it belonged to the Prophet (ﷺ), and after him it is for the benefit of the Muslims. ﴿So to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveler﴾. The meaning of "to Allah" is that He judges concerning it as He wills. "To the Messenger" means it becomes his possession. "To the near relatives" refers to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because they were prevented from receiving zakat, so a share of the fay' was given to them.

It has been said: The division of this property is such that four-fifths belong to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and its one-fifth is divided into five parts: one part for the Messenger, and one part for each of the four categories mentioned. It has also been said that it is divided into six parts.

The sixth is the share of Allah, the Exalted, and it is spent on the avenues of nearness to Allah, such as the upkeep of mosques and the like. ﴿So that it does not become a circulation among the rich among you﴾. That is, so that the fay' does not become a circulation confined to the rich, excluding the poor. Dawlah is the name for a thing that people pass around among themselves, so that it belongs to this one at one time and to that one at another time.

Muqatil said: The meaning is that the rich overpower the poor and then divide it among themselves.

The majority read yakun with the ya' (third person), and dawlah in the accusative, meaning: so that the fay' does not become a dawlah.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Hisham and Abu Hayyan read it as takun with the ta' (feminine), and dawlah in the nominative, meaning: so that a dawlah does not occur or come into being; here kana is used as a complete verb.

The majority read dawlah with a damma on the dal.

Abu Haywah and al-Sulami read it with a fatha on the dal.

'Isa ibn 'Umar, Yunus and al-Asma'i said: They are two dialects with one meaning.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: Dawlah with a fatha is that which is passed around among the property, and with a damma it is the action.

Abu 'Ubaydah also said the same.

Then, when He, the Exalted, had explained to them the destinations of this property, He commanded them to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. That is: whatever he gives you from the property of spoils, take it, and whatever he forbids you from taking, refrain from it and do not take it.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: Whatever he gives you from the property of the fay', accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it.

Ibn Juraij said: Whatever he brings you of obedience to Me, do it, and whatever he forbids you of disobedience to Me, avoid it.

The truth is that this verse is general to everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brings, whether a command, a prohibition, a saying or an action.

And even if the occasion of revelation is specific, what is taken into account is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

Everything that he has brought to us of the Shari'ah, he has given to us and conveyed to us.

How beneficial this verse is, and how great its benefit is.

Then, when He had commanded them to take what the Messenger commanded them and to leave what he forbade them, He commanded them to be mindful of Him and warned them of the severity of His punishment.

He said: ﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾. So He punishes whoever does not take what the Messenger brought and does not refrain from what he forbade.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The expedition of the Banu al-Nadir, who were a group of the Jews, took place six months after the Battle of Badr. Their dwelling and their palm trees were in the outskirts of Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged them until they agreed to depart, and on condition that they could take with them whatever the camels could carry of goods and property, except the hilqah, meaning weapons. So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿For the first gathering. You did not think that they would leave﴾. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) fought them until they made peace with him on the condition of exile, and he sent them to Syria. They were from a tribe that had not previously been exiled, and Allah had decreed this upon them. Had it not been for that, He would have punished them in this world by killing and captivity.

As for His saying, ﴿for the first gathering﴾, their exile was the first gathering in this world, to Syria.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: Whoever doubts that the place of gathering is in Syria, let him recite this verse: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them on that day: Depart! They said: To where? He said: To the land of the gathering.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had besieged them until he had inflicted on them every kind of hardship. So they gave him what he wanted from them, and he made peace with them on the condition that he would spare their lives, that he would expel them from their land and homelands, and that they would travel to Adhri'at in Syria. He gave each three of them one camel and one water-skin.

In al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned and cut down the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir, and it was at al-Buwayrah, and Hassan said concerning it:

"It was humiliating to the nobles of the Banu Lu'ayy
A burning at al-Buwayrah, spreading far."

Then Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse: He said: Al-linah is the palm tree. ﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾. He said: They forced them down from their fortresses and ordered the cutting of the palm trees, and this stirred something in their hearts. The Muslims said: We have cut down some and left some, so let us ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Is there a reward for us in what we cut down, and is there a sin upon us for what we left? So Allah revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, the verse. There are also other hadiths on this subject. The account of the treaty with the Banu al-Nadir is expounded in the books of biography (sirah).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah restored to His Messenger, from which the Muslims did not advance with horses or camels, and it was specifically for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He used to spend from it on his family the provision of a year, and then he would place what remained in weapons and horses as preparation for the cause of Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿You did not advance against it with horses or camels﴾: So what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acquired, he would judge concerning it as he wished, and there were no horses or camels on that day that could be advanced with.

He said: The ijafah (advancing) is pressing the pace. And it belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). From that were Khaybar, Fadak and the villages of 'Uraynah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to head for Yanbu', and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went there and took possession of all of it. Some people said: Why did Allah not divide it? So Allah revealed His excuse, saying: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: What Allah restored to His Messenger from Khaybar was half for Allah and His Messenger, and the other half for the Muslims. What belonged to Allah and His Messenger from it were al-Kathibah, al-Wati', Salalim and Wajrah. What belonged to the Muslims was the Shiqq, and the Shiqq was thirteen shares, and Natah was five shares. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not divide anything from Khaybar among the Muslims except for those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not permit any of the Muslims who had stayed behind from him when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah to attend Khaybar with him, except Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari.

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had choice property (safaya) from al-Nadir, Khaybar and Fadak. As for the Banu al-Nadir, it was held in reserve for his emergencies. As for Fadak, it was for the wayfarer. As for Khaybar, he divided it into three parts: he distributed two parts among the Muslims, and he kept one part for himself and for the provision of his family. Whatever remained beyond his family's provision, he returned to the poor among the Muhajirun.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Zanjawayh in al-Amwal, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: There is no Muslim on the face of the earth except that he has a right in this fay', except what your right hands possess.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and the women who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair, and the women who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah. This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub. She came to Ibn Mas'ud and said: It has reached me that you have cursed so-and-so and so-and-so. He said: And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah? She said: I have read what is between the two covers (of the Qur'an) and I did not find anything of this in it. He said: If you had read it, you would have found it. Did you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾? She said: Yes. He said: Then he has forbidden it.

[p. 1475]

His saying "for the poor" (lil-fuqara'): it was said that it is a substitute (badal) for "for the near relatives" and what is conjoined to it. It cannot be a substitute for "the Messenger" and what follows, lest it entail describing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as poor. It was also said that the implied meaning is "so that it does not become a circulating wealth (dawlah), but it is for the poor." It was said that the implied meaning is "be amazed at the poor." It was said that the implied meaning is: "and Allah is severe in punishment, for the poor," i.e., He is severe in punishment toward the disbelievers because of the poor. It was also said that it is a conjunction to what preceded, with the particle "and" (wa) understood, as you say: "the wealth is for Zayd, for ʿAmr, for Bakr." By "the emigrants" (al-Muhajirin) is meant those who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) out of desire for the religion and in support of him.

Qatadah said: These emigrants are those who abandoned their homes, their wealth, and their families. The meaning of ﴿they were expelled from their homes﴾ is that the disbelievers of Makkah expelled them from it and compelled them to leave. They were a hundred men, ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure﴾, i.e., they seek from Him that He bestow favor upon them with provision in this world and with good pleasure in the Hereafter, ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾ by striving against the disbelievers. This clause is conjoined to "seeking," and the position of both clauses is accusative as circumstantial clauses (hal): the first is concurrent (muqarinah), and the second is anticipated (muqaddarah), i.e., intending that. It is also permissible for it to be a concurrent circumstantial clause, because their departure in that state is support for Allah and His Messenger. The indication in his saying ﴿those﴾ refers to them in respect of their being characterized by those qualities. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (p-1476) ﴿they are the truthful﴾, i.e., those who are complete in truthfulness and firmly established in it.

Then, when he had finished praising the emigrants, he praised the Helpers (al-Ansar), saying: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and in faith before them﴾. By "the abode" is meant Madinah, which is the abode of emigration (dar al-hijrah). The meaning of their "settling" (tabawwu') in the abode and in faith is that they took it as a dwelling place (mabaʾah), i.e., they became firmly established in it with great firmness. Tabawwu' in its original usage applies only to a place, but He made faith like it because of their being firmly established in it, treating the state as if it were the place. It was said that "faith" is governed by a verb other than the one mentioned, and the implied meaning is: "and they adhered to faith," or "and they sincerely held faith." So said Abu ʿAli al-Farisi.

It is also permissible that it is by deletion of a modifier (mudaf), i.e., "they settled in the abode and in the place of faith." It is also permissible that "tabawwu'" is taken to imply the meaning of "lazimu" (they adhered), and the implied meaning is: "they adhered to the abode and to faith." The meaning of ﴿before them﴾ is: before the emigration of the emigrants. So a modifier must be implied, because the Helpers only believed after the faith of the emigrants. The relative clause is a subject, and its predicate is ﴿they love those who emigrate to them﴾. That is because they treated the emigrants well, made them partners in their wealth and dwellings, ﴿and they do not find in their breasts any need﴾, i.e., the Helpers do not find in their breasts envy, rage, or resentment regarding what was given (utu) to the emigrants, i.e., what was given to the emigrants to the exclusion of them from the spoils (fay'), but rather their souls were content with that.

In the speech there is a deleted modifier: i.e., they do not find in their breasts the touch of a need or the trace of a need. Everything a person finds in his breast of what he needs is a "need" (hajah).

The emigrants were residing in the homes of the Helpers. When the Prophet (ﷺ) took the Banu al-Nadir as spoils, he summoned the Helpers and thanked them for what they had done with the emigrants by housing them in their dwellings and making them partners in their wealth. Then he said: "If you wish, I will divide what Allah has given me as spoils from the Banu al-Nadir between you and the emigrants, and the emigrants will remain in the state they are in, dwelling in your homes and sharing your wealth; and if you wish, I will give them that and they will leave your homes." So they consented to the division of that among the emigrants, and their souls were content. ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾. Preference (al-ithar) is placing another before oneself in the matters of worldly portions, out of desire for the portions of the Hereafter. It is said: "I preferred him with such-and-such," i.e., I singled him out with it. The meaning is: they give precedence to the emigrants over themselves in worldly portions. ﴿Even though they themselves were in need﴾, i.e., want and poverty. Khasasah is derived from the "khisas" of the house, which are the gaps that exist in it. The clause "even though they were in need" is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause. It was said that khasasah is derived from "ikhtisas," which is singling oneself out with a matter, so khasasah is singling oneself out with need. From this is the saying of the poet:

When spring becomes a khasasah, the sick man lives by it, and the poor man grows rich.

﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾. The majority read yuqa with a sukun on the waw and a light qaf, from al-wiqayah (protection). Ibn Abi ʿAblah and Abu Haywah read it with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the qaf. The majority read ﴿shuhha nafsihi﴾ with a damma on the shin. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it with a kasra. Al-shuhh is stinginess together with greed, so stated in al-Sihah. It was said that al-shuhh is more severe than al-bukhl (miserliness). Muqatil said: "the stinginess of his soul" is the greed of his soul. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the stinginess of the soul is taking what is unlawful and withholding zakat. Ibn Zayd said: whoever takes nothing that Allah has forbidden him, and withholds nothing that Allah has commanded him to pay, has been protected from the stinginess of his soul. Tawus said: al-bukhl is that a person is stingy with what is in his hand, and al-shuhh is that he is greedy for what is in the hands of people, wanting to have what is in their hands by lawful and unlawful means, and is never content. Ibn ʿUyaynah said: al-shuhh is injustice. Al-Layth said: it is abandoning obligations and violating prohibitions.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that success is contingent upon the absence of the soul's stinginess regarding anything that the Law considers reprehensible to withhold, such as zakat, charity, maintaining kinship ties, or the like, as indicated by the attribution of stinginess to the soul. The indication in his saying ﴿those﴾ refers to "whoever" in respect of its meaning. It is a subject, and its predicate is ﴿they are the successful﴾. Al-falah is winning and attaining every desired thing.

Then, when He (glory be to Him) had finished praising the emigrants and the Helpers, He mentioned what those who came after them should say, saying: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and they are the followers of them in goodness until the Day of Resurrection. It was said: they are those who emigrated after Islam had grown strong. The apparent meaning of the verse includes those who came after the foremost, from among the Companions whose Islam came later in the era of prophethood, and whoever followed them among the Muslims after the era of prophethood until the Day of Resurrection, because it applies to all of them that they came after the first emigrants and the Helpers. The relative clause is a subject, and its predicate is ﴿they say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾. It is permissible that the relative clause is conjoined to His saying ﴿and those who settled in the abode and in faith﴾, so "they say" would be in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or it is a resumed statement with no position. By "brotherhood" here is meant brotherhood in religion. Allah commanded them to seek forgiveness for themselves and for those who preceded them among the emigrants and the Helpers. ﴿And do not place in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe﴾, i.e., malice, hatred, and envy.

After the seeking of forgiveness for the emigrants and the Helpers, Allah (glory be to Him) commanded them to ask Him to remove from their hearts rancor toward those who believe, without restriction. Thereby the Companions enter into this in the first place, because they are the most noble of the believers, and because the context concerns them. So whoever does not seek forgiveness for the Companions in general and ask for Allah's good pleasure for them has opposed what Allah commanded in this verse. If he finds in his heart rancor toward them, then he has been touched by a prick from Satan, and a considerable share of disobedience to Allah has befallen him, by enmity toward the allies of Allah and the best of the community of His Prophet (ﷺ), and a door of abandonment has opened for him, by which he will go down to the fire of Hell unless he corrects himself by turning to Allah (glory be to Him) and seeking His help, by asking Him to remove from his heart the rancor that has crept into it toward the best generations and the most noble of this community. If he goes beyond the rancor he finds to reviling any one of them, then he has submitted to Satan with a leash and has fallen into the anger and wrath of Allah. This incurable disease only afflicts one who is afflicted with a teacher from among the Rafidah, or a companion from among the enemies of the best of the community, those whom Satan has toyed with and whom he has adorned with various falsehoods, fabricated tales, and invented superstitions, and has turned them away from the Book of Allah, to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it, and from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) transmitted to us (p-1477) through the narrations of the great imams in every era. So they bought error in exchange for guidance, and exchanged great loss for abundant profit. Satan the accursed continued to move them from station to station and from rank to rank until they became enemies of the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, the best of His community, His righteous servants, and all the believers. They neglected the obligations of Allah and abandoned the rites of the religion. They strove with all their effort against Islam and its people, and they hurled at the religion and its people every stone and clod. Allah encompasses them from behind. ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful﴾, i.e., most abundant in kindness and mercy, and most eloquent in both, toward whoever among Your servants deserves that.

Al-Bukhari transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I enjoin upon the caliph after me the first emigrants, that he recognize their right and preserve their sanctity; and I enjoin upon him the Helpers, those who settled in the abode and in faith before them, that he accept from their good-doers and overlook their wrongdoers."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, hunger has afflicted me. So he sent to his wives, but found nothing with them. He said: 'Is there not a man who will host this one tonight? May Allah have mercy on him.' A man from the Helpers said, and in another narration Abu Talhah al-Ansari said: 'I, O Messenger of Allah.' So he took him to his household and said to his wife: 'Honor the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), do not withhold anything from him.' She said: 'By Allah, I have nothing except the food of the children.' He said: 'When the children want supper, put them to sleep, come and extinguish the lamp, and we will go hungry tonight for the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She did so. Then the guest went to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the morning, and he said: 'Allah has marveled tonight at so-and-so and so-and-so,' and He sent down concerning them: ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar who said: "A head of a sheep was sent as a gift to a man from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'My brother so-and-so and his dependents are more in need of this than we are,' so he sent it to him. Then that one kept sending it to another, until the people of seven households passed it around, until it returned to the first. So concerning them was revealed: ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab transmitted from Ibn Masʿud that a man said: "I fear that I have perished." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "I heard Allah say: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, and I am a stingy man, nothing from me scarcely comes out." Ibn Masʿud said to him: "That is not stinginess, rather it is miserliness, and there is no good in miserliness. Indeed, the stinginess that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an is that you eat the wealth of your brother unjustly."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar concerning the verse that he said: "Stinginess is not that a man withholds his wealth, rather it is miserliness, and that is indeed evil. Stinginess is only that a man's eye longs for what is not his."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: "Whoever pays the zakat of his wealth has been protected from the stinginess of his soul."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Yaʿla, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing has ever destroyed Islam like the destruction caused by stinginess."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Muslim, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of injustice, for injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection. And beware of stinginess, for stinginess destroyed those before you; it drove them to shed their blood and to make lawful their prohibitions."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 59, verses 8–10 (part 2 of 2):

Many ahadith have been transmitted condemning stinginess (shuhh).

Al-Hakim related it and declared it sound (sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh related it, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "People are in three stations. Two stations have passed and one station remains. The best that you can be upon is to be in this remaining station." Then he recited: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and Ibn Mardawayh related it from A'ishah, who said: "They were commanded to seek forgiveness for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), but they reviled them." Then she recited this verse: ﴿And those who came after them﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar that he heard a man disparaging some of the Emigrants (muhajirun). He recited to him: ﴿For the poor Emigrants﴾, the verse, then said: "These are the Emigrants. Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and the faith﴾, the verse. Then he said: "These are the Helpers (ansar). Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse, and then said: "Are you among these?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "None who reviles these is among them."

Ibn Abi ʿAblah and Abu Haywah read it with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the qaf. The majority read ﴿shuhha nafsihi﴾ with a damma on the shin. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it with a kasra. Ibn Zayd said: whoever takes nothing that Allah has forbidden him, and withholds nothing that Allah has commanded him to pay, has been protected from the stinginess of his soul. Tawus said: al-bukhl is that a person is stingy with what is in his hand, and al-shuhh is that he is greedy for what is in the hands of people, wanting to have what is in their hands by lawful and unlawful means, and is never content. Ibn ʿUyaynah said: al-shuhh is injustice. Al-Layth said: it is abandoning obligations and violating prohibitions.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that success is contingent upon the absence of the soul's stinginess regarding anything that the Law considers reprehensible to withhold, such as zakat, charity, maintaining kinship ties, or the like, as indicated by the attribution of stinginess to the soul. The indication in his saying ﴿those﴾ refers to "whoever" in respect of its meaning. It is a subject, and its predicate is ﴿they are the successful﴾. Al-falah is winning and attaining every desired thing.

By "brotherhood" here is meant brotherhood in religion. Allah commanded them to seek forgiveness for themselves and for those who preceded them among the emigrants and the Helpers. ﴿And do not place in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe﴾, i.e., malice, hatred, and envy.

After the seeking of forgiveness for the emigrants and the Helpers, Allah (glory be to Him) commanded them to ask Him to remove from their hearts rancor toward those who believe, without restriction. Thereby the Companions enter into this in the first place, because they are the most noble of the believers, and because the context concerns them. So whoever does not seek forgiveness for the Companions in general and ask for Allah's good pleasure for them has opposed what Allah commanded in this verse. If he finds in his heart rancor toward them, then he has been touched by a prick from Satan, and a considerable share of disobedience to Allah has befallen him, by enmity toward the allies of Allah and the best of the community of His Prophet (ﷺ), and a door of abandonment has opened for him, by which he will go down to the fire of Hell unless he corrects himself by turning to Allah (glory be to Him) and seeking His help, by asking Him to remove from his heart the rancor that has crept into it toward the best generations and the most noble of this community. If he goes beyond the rancor he finds to reviling any one of them, then he has submitted to Satan with a leash and has fallen into the anger and wrath of Allah. This incurable disease only afflicts one who is afflicted with a teacher from among the Rafidah, or a companion from among the enemies of the best of the community, those whom Satan has toyed with and whom he has adorned with various falsehoods, fabricated tales, and invented superstitions, and has turned them away from the Book of Allah, to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it, and from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) transmitted to us (p-1477) through the narrations of the great imams in every era. Satan the accursed continued to move them from station to station and from rank to rank until they became enemies of the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, the best of His community, His righteous servants, and all the believers. They neglected the obligations of Allah and abandoned the rites of the religion. They strove with all their effort against Islam and its people, and they hurled at the religion and its people every stone and clod. Allah encompasses them from behind. ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful﴾, i.e., most abundant in kindness and mercy, and most eloquent in both, toward whoever among Your servants deserves that.

Al-Bukhari transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I enjoin upon the caliph after me the first emigrants, that he recognize their right and preserve their sanctity; and I enjoin upon him the Helpers, those who settled in the abode and in faith before them, that he accept from their good-doers and overlook their wrongdoers."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, hunger has afflicted me. So he sent to his wives, but found nothing with them. He said: 'Is there not a man who will host this one tonight? May Allah have mercy on him.' A man from the Helpers said, and in another narration Abu Talhah al-Ansari said: 'I, O Messenger of Allah.' So he took him to his household and said to his wife: 'Honor the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), do not withhold anything from him.' She said: 'By Allah, I have nothing except the food of the children.' He said: 'When the children want supper, put them to sleep, come and extinguish the lamp, and we will go hungry tonight for the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She did so. Then the guest went to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the morning, and he said: 'Allah has marveled tonight at so-and-so and so-and-so,' and He sent down concerning them: ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar who said: "A head of a sheep was sent as a gift to a man from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'My brother so-and-so and his dependents are more in need of this than we are,' so he sent it to him. Then that one kept sending it to another, until the people of seven households passed it around, until it returned to the first. So concerning them was revealed: ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab transmitted from Ibn Masʿud that a man said: "I fear that I have perished." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "I heard Allah say: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, and I am a stingy man, nothing from me scarcely comes out." Ibn Masʿud said to him: "That is not stinginess, rather it is miserliness, and there is no good in miserliness. Indeed, the stinginess that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an is that you eat the wealth of your brother unjustly."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar concerning the verse that he said: "Stinginess is not that a man withholds his wealth, rather it is miserliness, and that is indeed evil. Stinginess is only that a man's eye longs for what is not his."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: "Whoever pays the zakat of his wealth has been protected from the stinginess of his soul."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Yaʿla, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing has ever destroyed Islam like the destruction caused by stinginess."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Muslim, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of injustice, for injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection. And beware of stinginess, for stinginess destroyed those before you; it drove them to shed their blood and to make lawful their prohibitions."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 59, verses 8–10 (part 2 of 2):

Many ahadith have been transmitted condemning stinginess (shuhh).

Al-Hakim related it and declared it sound (sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh related it, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "People are in three stations. Two stations have passed and one station remains. The best that you can be upon is to be in this remaining station." Then he recited: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and Ibn Mardawayh related it from A'ishah, who said: "They were commanded to seek forgiveness for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), but they reviled them." Then she recited this verse: ﴿And those who came after them﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar that he heard a man disparaging some of the Emigrants (muhajirun). He recited to him: ﴿For the poor Emigrants﴾, the verse, then said: "These are the Emigrants. Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and the faith﴾, the verse. Then he said: "These are the Helpers (ansar). Are you one of them?" He said: "No." Then he recited to him: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse, and then said: "Are you among these?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "None who reviles these is among them."

His saying "for the poor" (lil-fuqara'): it was said that it is a substitute (badal) for "for the near relatives" and what is conjoined to it. It cannot be a substitute for "the Messenger" and what follows, lest it entail describing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as poor. It was also said that the implied meaning is "so that it does not become a circulating wealth (dawlah), but it is for the poor." It was said that the implied meaning is "be amazed at the poor." It was said that the implied meaning is: "and Allah is severe in punishment, for the poor," i.e., He is severe in punishment toward the disbelievers because of the poor. It was also said that it is a conjunction to what preceded, with the particle "and" (wa) understood, as you say: "the wealth is for Zayd, for ʿAmr, for Bakr." By "the emigrants" (al-Muhajirin) is meant those who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) out of desire for the religion and in support of him.

Qatadah said: These emigrants are those who abandoned their homes, their wealth, and their families. The meaning of ﴿they were expelled from their homes﴾ is that the disbelievers of Makkah expelled them from it and compelled them to leave. They were a hundred men, ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure﴾, i.e., they seek from Him that He bestow favor upon them with provision in this world and with good pleasure in the Hereafter, ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾ by striving against the disbelievers. This clause is conjoined to "seeking," and the position of both clauses is accusative as circumstantial clauses (hal): the first is concurrent (muqarinah), and the second is anticipated (muqaddarah), i.e., intending that. It is also permissible for it to be a concurrent circumstantial clause, because their departure in that state is support for Allah and His Messenger. The indication in his saying ﴿those﴾ refers to them in respect of their being characterized by those qualities. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (p-1476) ﴿they are the truthful﴾, i.e., those who are complete in truthfulness and firmly established in it.

Then, when he had finished praising the emigrants, he praised the Helpers (al-Ansar), saying: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and in faith before them﴾. By "the abode" is meant Madinah, which is the abode of emigration (dar al-hijrah). The meaning of their "settling" (tabawwu') in the abode and in faith is that they took it as a dwelling place (mabaʾah), i.e., they became firmly established in it with great firmness. Tabawwu' in its original usage applies only to a place, but He made faith like it because of their being firmly established in it, treating the state as if it were the place. It was said that "faith" is governed by a verb other than the one mentioned, and the implied meaning is: "and they adhered to faith," or "and they sincerely held faith." So said Abu ʿAli al-Farisi.

It is also permissible that it is by deletion of a modifier (mudaf), i.e., "they settled in the abode and in the place of faith." It is also permissible that "tabawwu'" is taken to imply the meaning of "lazimu" (they adhered), and the implied meaning is: "they adhered to the abode and to faith." The meaning of ﴿before them﴾ is: before the emigration of the emigrants. So a modifier must be implied, because the Helpers only believed after the faith of the emigrants. The relative clause is a subject, and its predicate is ﴿they love those who emigrate to them﴾. That is because they treated the emigrants well, made them partners in their wealth and dwellings, ﴿and they do not find in their breasts any need﴾, i.e., the Helpers do not find in their breasts envy, rage, or resentment regarding what was given (utu) to the emigrants, i.e., what was given to the emigrants to the exclusion of them from the spoils (fay'), but rather their souls were content with that.

In the speech there is a deleted modifier: i.e., they do not find in their breasts the touch of a need or the trace of a need. Everything a person finds in his breast of what he needs is a "need" (hajah).

The emigrants were residing in the homes of the Helpers. When the Prophet (ﷺ) took the Banu al-Nadir as spoils, he summoned the Helpers and thanked them for what they had done with the emigrants by housing them in their dwellings and making them partners in their wealth. Then he said: "If you wish, I will divide what Allah has given me as spoils from the Banu al-Nadir between you and the emigrants, and the emigrants will remain in the state they are in, dwelling in your homes and sharing your wealth; and if you wish, I will give them that and they will leave your homes." So they consented to the division of that among the emigrants, and their souls were content. ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in need﴾. Preference (al-ithar) is placing another before oneself in the matters of worldly portions, out of desire for the portions of the Hereafter. It is said: "I preferred him with such-and-such," i.e., I singled him out with it. The meaning is: they give precedence to the emigrants over themselves in worldly portions. ﴿Even though they themselves were in need﴾, i.e., want and poverty. Khasasah is derived from the "khisas" of the house, which are the gaps that exist in it. The clause "even though they were in need" is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause. It was said that khasasah is derived from "ikhtisas," which is singling oneself out with a matter, so khasasah is singling oneself out with need. From this is the saying of the poet:

When spring becomes a khasasah, the sick man lives by it, and the poor man grows rich.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 59, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, finished mentioning the three categories of believers, He mentioned what took place between the hypocrites (munafiqun) and the Jews by way of their speech, so as to make the believers marvel at their condition. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite?﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah, or to anyone suitable for it. The ones who played the hypocrite were Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. The clause ﴿they say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is a resumed clause (mustanfa'a) explaining what is being marvelled at. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is either to bring the scene vividly before the mind or to indicate continuity (al-istimrar). He made them "brothers" to them because disbelief had united them, and although the kind of their disbelief differed, they are brothers in disbelief. The lam in ﴿li-ikhwanihim﴾ is the lam of conveying (lam al-tabligh, the lam that introduces the one addressed). It is said that this is the speech of Banu al-Nadir to Banu Qurayza, but the first view is preferable, because Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza are both Jews, while the hypocrites are other than them. The lam in His words ﴿If you are expelled﴾ is the preparatory lam for an oath (lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam), meaning: "By Allah, if you are expelled from your homes, we will surely go out with you." This is the answer of the oath: "we will surely go out from our homes in your company." ﴿And we will not obey anyone concerning you﴾ meaning, concerning your affair and on your account, anyone who wants to prevent us from going out with you, however long the time may be. This is the meaning of His words: "ever." Then, when they promised them to go out with them, they promised them support, saying: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ against your enemy.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, denied them, saying: ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in what they promised them of going out with them and supporting them.

Then, when He summarized their lying in what they promised, He detailed what they lied about, saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not support them﴾. The matter was indeed so, for the hypocrites did not go out with those of the Jews who were expelled, namely Banu al-Nadir and those with them, and they did not support those of the Jews who were fought, namely Banu Qurayza and the people of Khaybar. ﴿And if they should support them﴾ meaning, supposing that their support of them were to occur, because what Allah has negated cannot come to exist.

﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah﴾, meaning: indeed you, O assembly of Muslims, are more fearful and more awed in the breasts of the hypocrites, or the breasts of the Jews, or the breasts of all of them, than Allah is; that is, [you are more feared] than the fear of Allah. Had they had understanding, they would have known that Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who gave you power over them, so He is more deserving of fear from them than you.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of their additional cowardice and the weakness of their attack, saying: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites will not come out united to fight you, and they are not able to do so except in fortified villages, protected by fortifications and houses. ﴿Or from behind walls﴾, meaning from behind the walls behind which they hide out of their cowardice and fear.

The majority of readers read ﴿judur﴾ in the plural. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ﴿jidar﴾ in the singular.

Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, because it agrees with His words ﴿fortified villages﴾.

Some Meccan readers read ﴿jadr﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect form for "wall" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾, meaning: some of them are harsh and rough toward others; their hearts are divergent and their intentions are dissimilar.

Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the divergence of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter.

Mujahid said: ﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾ means through speech and threats, such as "he will surely do such and such."

The meaning is that when they are alone they attribute to themselves strength and might, but when they meet an enemy they are humbled, submit, and are defeated. It was also said: the meaning is that their might compared to their equals is intense, and their weakness is only in relation to you, because of the terror Allah has cast into their hearts. The first view is preferable, because of His words: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾, for this indicates that their gathering is only outward while their hearts are at odds inwardly, and this discord is the might among them, which is described as intense. It is also narrated from him that he said: what is meant is the hypocrites.

Al-Thawri said: they are the polytheists and the People of the Book.

Qatada said: ﴿You think them united﴾ means united upon a matter and an opinion, ﴿but their hearts are scattered﴾ means dispersed. The people of falsehood have divergent opinions, divergent testimonies, and divergent desires, yet they are united in enmity toward the people of truth.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-qulubuhum ashaddu﴾ (and their hearts are more intense), meaning more divergent.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning: that divergence and dispersion is due to their being a people who do not reason anything; had they reasoned, they would have recognized the truth and followed it.

﴿Like those before them﴾: meaning, their example is like the example of those before them. The meaning is: the example of the hypocrites and the Jews is like the example of those before them from the disbelieving polytheists, shortly, meaning in a near time. The accusative of ﴿shortly﴾ is as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning: they resemble them in a near time. It was also said: the governing element (al-'amil) in it is ﴿they tasted﴾, meaning: they tasted in a near time. The meaning of ﴿they tasted the evil of their affair﴾ is the evil consequence of their disbelief in this world, through their being killed on the day of Badr. This occurred six months before the expedition against Banu al-Nadir, as Mujahid and others said. It was also said: what is meant is Banu al-Nadir, where Allah gave power over them, as Qatada said. It was also said: it refers to the killing of Banu Qurayza, as al-Dahhak said. It was also said: it is general to everyone whom Allah took vengeance upon because of his disbelief. The first view is preferable. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on it.

I say: This does not indicate that this man is the one intended by the verse; rather, it indicates that he is among those to whom it applies.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Ibn Abbas in a longer form than this, and there is nothing in it that indicates he is the one intended by the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar to it from Ibn Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 59, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, finished mentioning the three categories of believers, He mentioned what took place between the hypocrites (munafiqun) and the Jews by way of their speech, so as to make the believers marvel at their condition. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite?﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah, or to anyone suitable for it. The ones who played the hypocrite were Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. The clause ﴿they say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is a resumed clause (mustanfa'a) explaining what is being marvelled at. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is either to bring the scene vividly before the mind or to indicate continuity (al-istimrar). He made them "brothers" to them because disbelief had united them, and although the kind of their disbelief differed, they are brothers in disbelief. The lam in ﴿li-ikhwanihim﴾ is the lam of conveying (lam al-tabligh, the lam that introduces the one addressed). It is said that this is the speech of Banu al-Nadir to Banu Qurayza, but the first view is preferable, because Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza are both Jews, while the hypocrites are other than them. The lam in His words ﴿If you are expelled﴾ is the preparatory lam for an oath (lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam), meaning: "By Allah, if you are expelled from your homes, we will surely go out with you." This is the answer of the oath: "we will surely go out from our homes in your company." ﴿And we will not obey anyone concerning you﴾ meaning, concerning your affair and on your account, anyone who wants to prevent us from going out with you, however long the time may be. This is the meaning of His words: "ever." Then, when they promised them to go out with them, they promised them support, saying: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ against your enemy.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, denied them, saying: ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in what they promised them of going out with them and supporting them.

Then, when He summarized their lying in what they promised, He detailed what they lied about, saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not support them﴾. The matter was indeed so, for the hypocrites did not go out with those of the Jews who were expelled, namely Banu al-Nadir and those with them, and they did not support those of the Jews who were fought, namely Banu Qurayza and the people of Khaybar. ﴿And if they should support them﴾ meaning, supposing that their support of them were to occur, because what Allah has negated cannot come to exist.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that if they intended to support the Jews, ﴿they would surely turn their backs, then they would not be helped﴾, meaning the Jews would not become helped when their helper is defeated, and they are the hypocrites. It was also said: it means the hypocrites will not become helped after that; rather, Allah will humiliate them and their hypocrisy will not benefit them. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: they will not support them willingly, and ﴿if they should support them﴾ unwillingly, they would turn their backs. It was said: the meaning of ﴿they will not support them﴾ is: they will not persist in supporting them. The first view is preferable, and this falls under the category of His words: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾.

﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah﴾, meaning: indeed you, O assembly of Muslims, are more fearful and more awed in the breasts of the hypocrites, or the breasts of the Jews, or the breasts of all of them, than Allah is; that is, [you are more feared] than the fear of Allah. The word "rahba" here means "being feared" (al-marhuwiyya), because it is a verbal noun from the passive form, and its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾, meaning: that mentioned fear, described as such, is due to their lack of understanding of anything. Had they had understanding, they would have known that Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who gave you power over them, so He is more deserving of fear from them than you.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of their additional cowardice and the weakness of their attack, saying: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites will not come out united to fight you, and they are not able to do so except in fortified villages, protected by fortifications and houses. ﴿Or from behind walls﴾, meaning from behind the walls behind which they hide out of their cowardice and fear.

The majority of readers read ﴿judur﴾ in the plural. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ﴿jidar﴾ in the singular.

Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, because it agrees with His words ﴿fortified villages﴾.

Some Meccan readers read ﴿jadr﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect form for "wall" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾, meaning: some of them are harsh and rough toward others; their hearts are divergent and their intentions are dissimilar.

Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the divergence of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter.

Mujahid said: ﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾ means through speech and threats, such as "he will surely do such and such."

The meaning is that when they are alone they attribute to themselves strength and might, but when they meet an enemy they are humbled, submit, and are defeated. It was also said: the meaning is that their might compared to their equals is intense, and their weakness is only in relation to you, because of the terror Allah has cast into their hearts. The first view is preferable, because of His words: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾, for this indicates that their gathering is only outward while their hearts are at odds inwardly, and this discord is the might among them, which is described as intense. The meaning of "shatta" is "dispersed." Mujahid said: it refers to the Jews and the hypocrites: "You think them united, but their hearts are scattered."

It is also narrated from him that he said: what is meant is the hypocrites.

Al-Thawri said: they are the polytheists and the People of the Book.

Qatada said: ﴿You think them united﴾ means united upon a matter and an opinion, ﴿but their hearts are scattered﴾ means dispersed. The people of falsehood have divergent opinions, divergent testimonies, and divergent desires, yet they are united in enmity toward the people of truth.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-qulubuhum ashaddu﴾ (and their hearts are more intense), meaning more divergent.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning: that divergence and dispersion is due to their being a people who do not reason anything; had they reasoned, they would have recognized the truth and followed it.

﴿Like those before them﴾: meaning, their example is like the example of those before them. The meaning is: the example of the hypocrites and the Jews is like the example of those before them from the disbelieving polytheists, shortly, meaning in a near time. The accusative of ﴿shortly﴾ is as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning: they resemble them in a near time. It was also said: the governing element (al-'amil) in it is ﴿they tasted﴾, meaning: they tasted in a near time. The meaning of ﴿they tasted the evil of their affair﴾ is the evil consequence of their disbelief in this world, through their being killed on the day of Badr. This occurred six months before the expedition against Banu al-Nadir, as Mujahid and others said. It was also said: what is meant is Banu al-Nadir, where Allah gave power over them, as Qatada said. It was also said: it refers to the killing of Banu Qurayza, as al-Dahhak said. It was also said: it is general to everyone whom Allah took vengeance upon because of his disbelief. The first view is preferable. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Then He set forth for the Jews and the hypocrites another parable, saying: ﴿Like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning their example in abandoning one another and in their failure to support one another. The phrase is either the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or another predicate for the subject assumed before His words ﴿like the example of those before them﴾, with the coordinating particle omitted, as you say: "You are knowledgeable, you are working, you are generous."

It was said: the first parable is specific to the Jews, and the second is specific to the hypocrites. It was also said: the second parable is an explanation of the first.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained the aspect of resemblance, saying: ﴿when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning: he incited him to disbelief, made it attractive to him, and drove him to it. The word "man" here means the category of whoever among the human species obeyed Satan. It was said: he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel whom Satan drove to disbelief, and he obeyed him. ﴿So when he disbelieved, he said, "Indeed, I am free of you"﴾, meaning: when man disbelieved, complying with Satan and accepting his enticement, Satan said, "Indeed, I am free of you." This will be said by him on the Day of Resurrection. The clause ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for his disassociation from man after his disbelief. It was also said: the word "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, but the first view is preferable.

Mujahid said: the word "man" here means all people, being deceived by Satan. It was said: Satan's words "Indeed, I fear Allah" are not literal; rather, they are said as a disclaimer from the man, and so they are an emphasis of his words "Indeed, I am free of you."

The majority read ﴿inni﴾ with a sukun on the yā'.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on it.

﴿So the outcome of both of them was that they would be in the Fire﴾. The majority read ﴿'aqibatahuma﴾ in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of "kana," and its subject is ﴿that they would be in the Fire﴾.

Al-Hasan and Amr ibn Ubayd read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with the predicate being what follows. The meaning: the outcome of Satan and that man who disbelieved is that both of them are heading to the Fire, abiding therein eternally. The majority read ﴿khalidayn﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn Ali, and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿khalidan﴾ in the nominative, as the predicate of "anna," with the adverbial phrase (zarf) connected to it. ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning eternal abiding in the Fire is the recompense of the wrongdoers, and these ones enter among them by a stronger entry.

Then He returned, glory be to Him, to addressing the believers with a good admonition, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, meaning: fear His punishment by doing what He has commanded you and abstaining from what He has forbidden you. ﴿And let a soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, meaning: let it look at what deeds it has sent forward for the Day of Resurrection. The Arabs use "tomorrow" as a metaphor for the future. It was also said: the mention of "tomorrow" is to alert to the nearness of the Hour. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: He repeated the command to fear Allah for emphasis. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, nothing of that is hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾, meaning: who abandoned His command, or did not esteem Him as He should be esteemed, or did not fear Him, or all of that. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾, meaning He made them forget themselves because of their forgetting Him, so they did not occupy themselves with the deeds that would save them from punishment, and they did not refrain from the sins that would bring them into it. Thus there is an omitted modifier in the speech: that is, He caused them to forget the shares of their own souls. Sufyan said: they forgot the right of Allah, so He made them forget the right of their own souls. It was also said: they forgot Allah in ease, so He made them forget themselves in hardships. ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning those who are complete in departing from obedience to Allah.

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise﴾ in excellence and rank. What is meant is the two groups in general, so whoever among the people of the Fire forgot Allah enters the group of the people of the Fire by a stronger entry, and those who feared Allah enter the group of the people of Paradise by a stronger entry, because the context concerns them. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already been covered in surah al-Ma'idah, surah al-Sajdah, and surah Sad.

Then Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, informed about the companions of Paradise, after negating equality between them and the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise, they are the attainers of success﴾, meaning those who triumph in every sought-after thing and are saved from every hated thing.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite?﴾, that he said: Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifa'a ibn Tabut, Abd Allah ibn Nabtal, Aws ibn Qayzi, and their brothers, Banu al-Nadir.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated from him: "A group from Banu Awf ibn al-Harith, among them Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Wadi'a ibn Malik, Suwayd, and Da'is, were sent to Banu al-Nadir, saying: 'Stand firm and hold out, for we will not hand you over. If you are fought, we will fight alongside you, and if you are expelled, we will go out with you.' So they waited for that support from them, but they did not do it. Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to expel them and to spare their blood, on the condition that they could carry whatever the camels could bear, except for the armor. He did so. A man among them would demolish his house, place it on the back of a camel, and set off with it. They went out to Khaybar, and some of them traveled to Syria."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His words ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾ that he said: "They are the polytheists."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that a man used to worship in a monastery (ṣawma'a), and that a woman had brothers. Something befell her, so they brought her to him, and his soul adorned her to him, so he had intercourse with her and she became pregnant. Then Satan came to him and said: "Kill her, for if they discover you, you will be disgraced." So he killed her and buried her. Then they came, seized him, and took him away. While they were walking, Satan came to him and said: "I am the one who adorned this for you. Prostrate to me one prostration and I will save you." So he prostrated to him. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Like the Satan, when he says to man, "Disbelieve."﴾ and the rest of the verse.
