Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 59, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, finished mentioning the three categories of believers, He mentioned what took place between the hypocrites (munafiqun) and the Jews by way of their speech, so as to make the believers marvel at their condition. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite?﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah, or to anyone suitable for it. The ones who played the hypocrite were Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. The clause ﴿they say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is a resumed clause (mustanfa'a) explaining what is being marvelled at. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is either to bring the scene vividly before the mind or to indicate continuity (al-istimrar). He made them "brothers" to them because disbelief had united them, and although the kind of their disbelief differed, they are brothers in disbelief. The lam in ﴿li-ikhwanihim﴾ is the lam of conveying (lam al-tabligh, the lam that introduces the one addressed). It is said that this is the speech of Banu al-Nadir to Banu Qurayza, but the first view is preferable, because Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza are both Jews, while the hypocrites are other than them. The lam in His words ﴿If you are expelled﴾ is the preparatory lam for an oath (lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam), meaning: "By Allah, if you are expelled from your homes, we will surely go out with you." This is the answer of the oath: "we will surely go out from our homes in your company." ﴿And we will not obey anyone concerning you﴾ meaning, concerning your affair and on your account, anyone who wants to prevent us from going out with you, however long the time may be. This is the meaning of His words: "ever." Then, when they promised them to go out with them, they promised them support, saying: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ against your enemy.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, denied them, saying: ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in what they promised them of going out with them and supporting them.

Then, when He summarized their lying in what they promised, He detailed what they lied about, saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not support them﴾. The matter was indeed so, for the hypocrites did not go out with those of the Jews who were expelled, namely Banu al-Nadir and those with them, and they did not support those of the Jews who were fought, namely Banu Qurayza and the people of Khaybar. ﴿And if they should support them﴾ meaning, supposing that their support of them were to occur, because what Allah has negated cannot come to exist.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that if they intended to support the Jews, ﴿they would surely turn their backs, then they would not be helped﴾, meaning the Jews would not become helped when their helper is defeated, and they are the hypocrites. It was also said: it means the hypocrites will not become helped after that; rather, Allah will humiliate them and their hypocrisy will not benefit them. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: they will not support them willingly, and ﴿if they should support them﴾ unwillingly, they would turn their backs. It was said: the meaning of ﴿they will not support them﴾ is: they will not persist in supporting them. The first view is preferable, and this falls under the category of His words: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾.

﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah﴾, meaning: indeed you, O assembly of Muslims, are more fearful and more awed in the breasts of the hypocrites, or the breasts of the Jews, or the breasts of all of them, than Allah is; that is, [you are more feared] than the fear of Allah. The word "rahba" here means "being feared" (al-marhuwiyya), because it is a verbal noun from the passive form, and its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾, meaning: that mentioned fear, described as such, is due to their lack of understanding of anything. Had they had understanding, they would have known that Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who gave you power over them, so He is more deserving of fear from them than you.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of their additional cowardice and the weakness of their attack, saying: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites will not come out united to fight you, and they are not able to do so except in fortified villages, protected by fortifications and houses. ﴿Or from behind walls﴾, meaning from behind the walls behind which they hide out of their cowardice and fear.

The majority of readers read ﴿judur﴾ in the plural. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ﴿jidar﴾ in the singular.

Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, because it agrees with His words ﴿fortified villages﴾.

Some Meccan readers read ﴿jadr﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect form for "wall" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾, meaning: some of them are harsh and rough toward others; their hearts are divergent and their intentions are dissimilar.

Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the divergence of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter.

Mujahid said: ﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾ means through speech and threats, such as "he will surely do such and such."

The meaning is that when they are alone they attribute to themselves strength and might, but when they meet an enemy they are humbled, submit, and are defeated. It was also said: the meaning is that their might compared to their equals is intense, and their weakness is only in relation to you, because of the terror Allah has cast into their hearts. The first view is preferable, because of His words: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾, for this indicates that their gathering is only outward while their hearts are at odds inwardly, and this discord is the might among them, which is described as intense. The meaning of "shatta" is "dispersed." Mujahid said: it refers to the Jews and the hypocrites: "You think them united, but their hearts are scattered."

It is also narrated from him that he said: what is meant is the hypocrites.

Al-Thawri said: they are the polytheists and the People of the Book.

Qatada said: ﴿You think them united﴾ means united upon a matter and an opinion, ﴿but their hearts are scattered﴾ means dispersed. The people of falsehood have divergent opinions, divergent testimonies, and divergent desires, yet they are united in enmity toward the people of truth.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-qulubuhum ashaddu﴾ (and their hearts are more intense), meaning more divergent.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning: that divergence and dispersion is due to their being a people who do not reason anything; had they reasoned, they would have recognized the truth and followed it.

﴿Like those before them﴾: meaning, their example is like the example of those before them. The meaning is: the example of the hypocrites and the Jews is like the example of those before them from the disbelieving polytheists, shortly, meaning in a near time. The accusative of ﴿shortly﴾ is as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning: they resemble them in a near time. It was also said: the governing element (al-'amil) in it is ﴿they tasted﴾, meaning: they tasted in a near time. The meaning of ﴿they tasted the evil of their affair﴾ is the evil consequence of their disbelief in this world, through their being killed on the day of Badr. This occurred six months before the expedition against Banu al-Nadir, as Mujahid and others said. It was also said: what is meant is Banu al-Nadir, where Allah gave power over them, as Qatada said. It was also said: it refers to the killing of Banu Qurayza, as al-Dahhak said. It was also said: it is general to everyone whom Allah took vengeance upon because of his disbelief. The first view is preferable. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Then He set forth for the Jews and the hypocrites another parable, saying: ﴿Like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning their example in abandoning one another and in their failure to support one another. The phrase is either the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or another predicate for the subject assumed before His words ﴿like the example of those before them﴾, with the coordinating particle omitted, as you say: "You are knowledgeable, you are working, you are generous."

It was said: the first parable is specific to the Jews, and the second is specific to the hypocrites. It was also said: the second parable is an explanation of the first.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained the aspect of resemblance, saying: ﴿when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning: he incited him to disbelief, made it attractive to him, and drove him to it. The word "man" here means the category of whoever among the human species obeyed Satan. It was said: he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel whom Satan drove to disbelief, and he obeyed him. ﴿So when he disbelieved, he said, "Indeed, I am free of you"﴾, meaning: when man disbelieved, complying with Satan and accepting his enticement, Satan said, "Indeed, I am free of you." It was also said: the word "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, but the first view is preferable.

Mujahid said: the word "man" here means all people, being deceived by Satan. It was said: Satan's words "Indeed, I fear Allah" are not literal; rather, they are said as a disclaimer from the man, and so they are an emphasis of his words "Indeed, I am free of you."

The majority read ﴿inni﴾ with a sukun on the yā'.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on it.

﴿So the outcome of both of them was that they would be in the Fire﴾. The majority read ﴿'aqibatahuma﴾ in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of "kana," and its subject is ﴿that they would be in the Fire﴾.

Al-Hasan and Amr ibn Ubayd read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with the predicate being what follows. The meaning: the outcome of Satan and that man who disbelieved is that both of them are heading to the Fire, abiding therein eternally. The majority read ﴿khalidayn﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn Ali, and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿khalidan﴾ in the nominative, as the predicate of "anna," with the adverbial phrase (zarf) connected to it. ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning eternal abiding in the Fire is the recompense of the wrongdoers, and these ones enter among them by a stronger entry.

Then He returned, glory be to Him, to addressing the believers with a good admonition, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, meaning: fear His punishment by doing what He has commanded you and abstaining from what He has forbidden you. ﴿And let a soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, meaning: let it look at what deeds it has sent forward for the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the mention of "tomorrow" is to alert to the nearness of the Hour. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: He repeated the command to fear Allah for emphasis. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, nothing of that is hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾, meaning: who abandoned His command, or did not esteem Him as He should be esteemed, or did not fear Him, or all of that. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾, meaning He made them forget themselves because of their forgetting Him, so they did not occupy themselves with the deeds that would save them from punishment, and they did not refrain from the sins that would bring them into it. Then Allah, glory be to Him, denied them, saying: ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in what they promised them of going out with them and supporting them.

Had they had understanding, they would have known that Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who gave you power over them, so He is more deserving of fear from them than you.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of their additional cowardice and the weakness of their attack, saying: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites will not come out united to fight you, and they are not able to do so except in fortified villages, protected by fortifications and houses. ﴿Or from behind walls﴾, meaning from behind the walls behind which they hide out of their cowardice and fear.

The majority of readers read ﴿judur﴾ in the plural. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ﴿jidar﴾ in the singular.

Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, because it agrees with His words ﴿fortified villages﴾.

Some Meccan readers read ﴿jadr﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect form for "wall" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾, meaning: some of them are harsh and rough toward others; their hearts are divergent and their intentions are dissimilar.

Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the divergence of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter.

Mujahid said: ﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾ means through speech and threats, such as "he will surely do such and such."

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that if they intended to support the Jews, ﴿they would surely turn their backs, then they would not be helped﴾, meaning the Jews would not become helped when their helper is defeated, and they are the hypocrites. It was also said: it means the hypocrites will not become helped after that; rather, Allah will humiliate them and their hypocrisy will not benefit them. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: they will not support them willingly, and ﴿if they should support them﴾ unwillingly, they would turn their backs. It was said: the meaning of ﴿they will not support them﴾ is: they will not persist in supporting them. The first view is preferable, and this falls under the category of His words: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾.

﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah﴾, meaning: indeed you, O assembly of Muslims, are more fearful and more awed in the breasts of the hypocrites, or the breasts of the Jews, or the breasts of all of them, than Allah is; that is, [you are more feared] than the fear of Allah. The word "rahba" here means "being feared" (al-marhuwiyya), because it is a verbal noun from the passive form, and its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾, meaning: that mentioned fear, described as such, is due to their lack of understanding of anything. Had they had understanding, they would have known that Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who gave you power over them, so He is more deserving of fear from them than you.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of their additional cowardice and the weakness of their attack, saying: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites will not come out united to fight you, and they are not able to do so except in fortified villages, protected by fortifications and houses. ﴿Or from behind walls﴾, meaning from behind the walls behind which they hide out of their cowardice and fear.

The majority of readers read ﴿judur﴾ in the plural. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ﴿jidar﴾ in the singular.

Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, because it agrees with His words ﴿fortified villages﴾.

Some Meccan readers read ﴿jadr﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect form for "wall" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾, meaning: some of them are harsh and rough toward others; their hearts are divergent and their intentions are dissimilar.

Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the divergence of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter.

Mujahid said: ﴿Their might among themselves is intense﴾ means through speech and threats, such as "he will surely do such and such."

The meaning is that when they are alone they attribute to themselves strength and might, but when they meet an enemy they are humbled, submit, and are defeated. It was also said: the meaning is that their might compared to their equals is intense, and their weakness is only in relation to you, because of the terror Allah has cast into their hearts. The first view is preferable, because of His words: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾, for this indicates that their gathering is only outward while their hearts are at odds inwardly, and this discord is the might among them, which is described as intense. The meaning of "shatta" is "dispersed." Mujahid said: it refers to the Jews and the hypocrites: "You think them united, but their hearts are scattered."

It is also narrated from him that he said: what is meant is the hypocrites.

Al-Thawri said: they are the polytheists and the People of the Book.

Qatada said: ﴿You think them united﴾ means united upon a matter and an opinion, ﴿but their hearts are scattered﴾ means dispersed. The people of falsehood have divergent opinions, divergent testimonies, and divergent desires, yet they are united in enmity toward the people of truth.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-qulubuhum ashaddu﴾ (and their hearts are more intense), meaning more divergent.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning: that divergence and dispersion is due to their being a people who do not reason anything; had they reasoned, they would have recognized the truth and followed it.

﴿Like those before them﴾: meaning, their example is like the example of those before them. The meaning is: the example of the hypocrites and the Jews is like the example of those before them from the disbelieving polytheists, shortly, meaning in a near time. The accusative of ﴿shortly﴾ is as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning: they resemble them in a near time. It was also said: the governing element (al-'amil) in it is ﴿they tasted﴾, meaning: they tasted in a near time. The meaning of ﴿they tasted the evil of their affair﴾ is the evil consequence of their disbelief in this world, through their being killed on the day of Badr. This occurred six months before the expedition against Banu al-Nadir, as Mujahid and others said. It was also said: what is meant is Banu al-Nadir, where Allah gave power over them, as Qatada said. It was also said: it refers to the killing of Banu Qurayza, as al-Dahhak said. It was also said: it is general to everyone whom Allah took vengeance upon because of his disbelief. The first view is preferable. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Then He set forth for the Jews and the hypocrites another parable, saying: ﴿Like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning their example in abandoning one another and in their failure to support one another. The phrase is either the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or another predicate for the subject assumed before His words ﴿like the example of those before them﴾, with the coordinating particle omitted, as you say: "You are knowledgeable, you are working, you are generous."

It was said: the first parable is specific to the Jews, and the second is specific to the hypocrites. It was also said: the second parable is an explanation of the first.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained the aspect of resemblance, saying: ﴿when he says to man, "Disbelieve"﴾, meaning: he incited him to disbelief, made it attractive to him, and drove him to it. The word "man" here means the category of whoever among the human species obeyed Satan. It was said: he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel whom Satan drove to disbelief, and he obeyed him. ﴿So when he disbelieved, he said, "Indeed, I am free of you"﴾, meaning: when man disbelieved, complying with Satan and accepting his enticement, Satan said, "Indeed, I am free of you." This will be said by him on the Day of Resurrection. The clause ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for his disassociation from man after his disbelief. It was also said: the word "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, but the first view is preferable.

Mujahid said: the word "man" here means all people, being deceived by Satan. It was said: Satan's words "Indeed, I fear Allah" are not literal; rather, they are said as a disclaimer from the man, and so they are an emphasis of his words "Indeed, I am free of you."

The majority read ﴿inni﴾ with a sukun on the yā'.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on it.

﴿So the outcome of both of them was that they would be in the Fire﴾. The majority read ﴿'aqibatahuma﴾ in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of "kana," and its subject is ﴿that they would be in the Fire﴾.

Al-Hasan and Amr ibn Ubayd read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with the predicate being what follows. The meaning: the outcome of Satan and that man who disbelieved is that both of them are heading to the Fire, abiding therein eternally. The majority read ﴿khalidayn﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn Ali, and Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿khalidan﴾ in the nominative, as the predicate of "anna," with the adverbial phrase (zarf) connected to it. ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning eternal abiding in the Fire is the recompense of the wrongdoers, and these ones enter among them by a stronger entry.

Then He returned, glory be to Him, to addressing the believers with a good admonition, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, meaning: fear His punishment by doing what He has commanded you and abstaining from what He has forbidden you. ﴿And let a soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, meaning: let it look at what deeds it has sent forward for the Day of Resurrection. The Arabs use "tomorrow" as a metaphor for the future. It was also said: the mention of "tomorrow" is to alert to the nearness of the Hour. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: He repeated the command to fear Allah for emphasis. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, nothing of that is hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾, meaning: who abandoned His command, or did not esteem Him as He should be esteemed, or did not fear Him, or all of that. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾, meaning He made them forget themselves because of their forgetting Him, so they did not occupy themselves with the deeds that would save them from punishment, and they did not refrain from the sins that would bring them into it. Thus there is an omitted modifier in the speech: that is, He caused them to forget the shares of their own souls. Sufyan said: they forgot the right of Allah, so He made them forget the right of their own souls. It was also said: they forgot Allah in ease, so He made them forget themselves in hardships. ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning those who are complete in departing from obedience to Allah.

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise﴾ in excellence and rank. What is meant is the two groups in general, so whoever among the people of the Fire forgot Allah enters the group of the people of the Fire by a stronger entry, and those who feared Allah enter the group of the people of Paradise by a stronger entry, because the context concerns them. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already been covered in surah al-Ma'idah, surah al-Sajdah, and surah Sad.

Then Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, informed about the companions of Paradise, after negating equality between them and the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise, they are the attainers of success﴾, meaning those who triumph in every sought-after thing and are saved from every hated thing.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite?﴾, that he said: Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifa'a ibn Tabut, Abd Allah ibn Nabtal, Aws ibn Qayzi, and their brothers, Banu al-Nadir.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated from him: "A group from Banu Awf ibn al-Harith, among them Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Wadi'a ibn Malik, Suwayd, and Da'is, were sent to Banu al-Nadir, saying: 'Stand firm and hold out, for we will not hand you over. If you are fought, we will fight alongside you, and if you are expelled, we will go out with you.' So they waited for that support from them, but they did not do it. Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to expel them and to spare their blood, on the condition that they could carry whatever the camels could bear, except for the armor. He did so. A man among them would demolish his house, place it on the back of a camel, and set off with it. They went out to Khaybar, and some of them traveled to Syria."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His words ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are scattered﴾ that he said: "They are the polytheists."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that a man used to worship in a monastery (ṣawma'a), and that a woman had brothers. Something befell her, so they brought her to him, and his soul adorned her to him, so he had intercourse with her and she became pregnant. Then Satan came to him and said: "Kill her, for if they discover you, you will be disgraced." So he killed her and buried her. Then they came, seized him, and took him away. While they were walking, Satan came to him and said: "I am the one who adorned this for you. Prostrate to me one prostration and I will save you." So he prostrated to him. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Like the Satan, when he says to man, "Disbelieve."﴾ and the rest of the verse.

I say: This does not indicate that this man is the one intended by the verse; rather, it indicates that he is among those to whom it applies.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Ibn Abbas in a longer form than this, and there is nothing in it that indicates he is the one intended by the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar to it from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿Like the Satan﴾, that he said: God struck the example of the disbelievers and hypocrites who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿like the Satan, when he says to man, "Disbelieve."﴾

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 59, verses 21–24:

When He, glorified is He, had finished mentioning the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and had shown that they are not equal in anything, He mentioned the greatness of His Noble Book, informed of its majesty, and that it is worthy that hearts should humble themselves before it and that hearts should be softened by it. So He said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbling itself, split asunder from the fear of Allah.﴾ That is: because of its status, its greatness, the excellence of its words, the strength of its structure, its eloquence, and its containing admonitions by which hearts are softened. [The meaning is that] if it were sent down upon one of the mountains that exist on the earth, you would see it, despite its extreme hardness (p-1480) and intense firmness and massive bulk, ﴿humbling itself, split apart﴾: that is, cracked from the fear of Allah, glorified is He, out of caution regarding His punishment and fear that it might not fulfil what is obligatory upon it of glorifying the speech of Allah. This is a figurative and imaginative illustration which implies the elevated status of the Qur'an and the strength of its effect upon hearts. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿And these are the parables We set forth for the people, that perhaps they may give thought﴾, so that they may reflect upon what is obligatory for them to reflect upon, in order that they may be admonished by the exhortations and restrained by the warnings. In this there is also a rebuke and reproach to the disbelievers, since they did not humble themselves before the Qur'an, nor were they admonished by its exhortations, nor were they restrained by its warnings. Al-khashi' (the humble one) is: the abased, the submissive.

It has also been said: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, O Muhammad, it would not have endured and would have split apart from its descent upon it. We have sent it down upon you, and We have made you firm for it and strengthened you to bear it. On this view it is an expression of favour toward the Prophet ﷺ, because Allah, glorified is He, made him steadfast for what the firm mountains could not bear.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of His lordship and His greatness, so He said: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾. In this is an affirmation of tawhid (the oneness of God) and a repelling of shirk (association of partners with Allah). ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: that is, Knower of what is hidden from the senses and what is present. It has been said: Knower of the secret and the open. It has been said: what has been and what will be. It has been said: the Hereafter and the world. He placed "the unseen" before "the witnessed" because it precedes it in existence. ﴿He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. The explanation of these two names has already preceded.

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾: He repeated it for emphasis and affirmation, since tawhid is deserving of that. ﴿The King, the Most Holy﴾: that is, the Pure, free from every defect, exalted above every deficiency. Al-quds, with the vowel on the first letter (al-qudus), in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz means the basin (saṭl), because one purifies oneself with it; and from it is al-qadus (a large vessel), the singular of the vessels by which water is drawn out.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read ﴿al-Quddus﴾ with a ḍamma on the qāf (qudus).

Abu Dharr and Abu al-Sammak read it with a fatha on it (qadus). Sibawayh used to say: sabbūḥ and qaddūs with a fatḥa on the first of them. Abu Hatim related from Ya'qub that he heard, in the presence of al-Kisa'i, a fluent Bedouin reading "al-qadus" with a fatha on the qāf.

Tha'lab said: every noun of the form faʿūl has a fatḥa on its first letter, except sabbūḥ and quddūs, for the ḍamma in them is more common, though both may be read with a fatḥa.

﴿As-Salam﴾: that is, the One who is free from every deficiency and defect. It has been said: the One who bestows peace upon His servants in Paradise, as He said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Yasin 58]. It has been said: the One from whom creation is safe from His injustice, and most of the scholars held this. It has been said: the One who grants safety to His servants, and it is a verbal noun described by it for emphasis. ﴿Al-Mu'min﴾: that is, the One who grants His servants safety from His punishment. It has been said: the One who confirms His messengers by manifesting miracles. It has been said: the One who confirms the believers in what He has promised them of reward and confirms the disbelievers in what He has threatened them with of punishment. It is said: amanahu (he granted him security) from al-amn, which is the opposite of fear. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And the Believer (al-mu'min), whose sanctuaries the birds wipe, the riders of Makkah between al-Ghayl and al-Sanad."

Mujahid said: al-Mu'min is the One who affirmed His own oneness by His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾.

Al-Jumhur read al-Mu'min with a kasra on the mim, an active participle from amana, in the sense of amina (to be secure).

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn read it with a fatha, in the sense of al-mu'man bihi (the one believed in), by elision, like His saying: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf 155]. Abu Hatim said: this reading is not permissible, because its meaning would be that he was fearful and someone else granted him security.

﴿Al-Muhaymin﴾: that is, the Witness over His servants regarding their deeds, the Watcher over them. Thus said Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil: it is said haymana yuhaymin, so he is muhaymin, when he is a watcher over a thing.

Al-Wahidi said: many of the exegetes held that its origin is mu'ayman, from amana yu'minu, so it would mean al-mu'min, but the first view is better. We have already discussed al-muhaymin in Surah al-Ma'idah.

﴿Al-'Aziz﴾: the One who has no equal. It has been said: the Subduer. It has been said: the Victorious, who is not overcome. It has been said: the Strong, the Compeller. Jabbar: the majesty of Allah is His greatness. The Arabs call a king jabbar. It may also be from jabara, when he enriches the poor and mends the broken. It may also be from jabarahu ʿala kadhā, when he compels him to what he wills; so He is the One who compelled His creation to what He wills from them. This was the view of al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Zajjaj preferred it, and al-Farra' said: it is from ajbarahu ʿala al-amr, meaning he forced him to it. He said: I have not heard fa''āl from af'ala except in jabbār from ajbara, and darrāk from adraka. It has also been said: al-Jabbar is the One whose might cannot be withstood.

﴿Al-Mutakabbir﴾: that is, the One who is exalted above every deficiency and magnified beyond what is not fitting for Him. The root of takabbur is refusal and not submitting. From it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"It has been effaced as the weaned calf effaces, and in it has become the pride of the stubborn, and it is now tame."

Pride (al-kibr) in the attributes of Allah is praise, and in the attributes of created beings it is blame.

Qatadah said: He is the One who is exalted above every evil.

Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Mutakabbir: the Possessor of greatness, who is the King.

Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the associating of the polytheists, so He said: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate﴾: that is, above what they associate with Him, or above their associating [others] with Him.

﴿He is Allah, the Creator﴾: that is, the One who determines things according to the requirement of His will and purpose. ﴿The Originator﴾: that is, the One who brings things into being, innovates them, and makes them exist. It has been said: the One who distinguishes some of them from others. ﴿The Fashioner﴾: that is, the One who brings forms into existence and composes them in various shapes. Tasywir (fashioning) follows upon khalq (creation) and bara' (origination) and is subsequent to them. The meaning of tasywir is outlining and shaping. Al-Nabigha said:

"The Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner in the wombs, from water until it becomes blood."

Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a Companion, read al-muṣawwar with a fatha on the waw and a fatha on the ra', as the object of al-bari' (the Originator): that is, the One who originated the fashioned one, meaning, He distinguished it.

﴿To Him belong the best names﴾: its explanation and discussion have already preceded in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the best names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 180].

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾: that is, whatever is in them declares Him free from imperfection, by the tongue of state or of speech. ﴿And He is the Almighty, the Wise﴾: that is, the Victorious over others, whom none can overcome, the Wise in all the matters by which He decrees.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾, that he said: it means, "Had I sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, which I had made it bear, it would have split and humbled itself from its weight and from the fear of Allah." So Allah commanded the people, when the Qur'an is revealed to them, to receive it with intense fear and humility. He said: Thus does Allah set forth parables for the people, that perhaps they may give thought.

(p-1481) Al-Daylami related from Ibn Mas'ud and Ali, in a marfu' report, regarding His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ to the end of the surah, that he said: it is a remedy for headache.

Al-Daylami narrated it with two chains, and we do not know the condition of their narrators.

Al-Khatib (al-Baghdadi) related in his History, with his chain, to Idris ibn Abd al-Karim al-Haddad, who said: I read to Khalaf, and when I reached this verse he said: Place your hand on your head, for I read to Hamzah, and when I reached this verse he said: Place your hand on your head, for I read to al-A'mash. Then he continued the chain in this manner, linked (musalsal), to Ibn Mas'ud, who said: I read to the Prophet ﷺ, and when I reached this verse he said to me: Place your hand on your head, for when Jibril descended with it, he said to me: Place your hand on your head, for it is a cure for every disease except al-sam, and al-sam is death.

Al-Dhahabi said: this is false.

Ibn al-Sunni in ʿAmal al-Yawm wa al-Layla and Ibn Mardawayh also related, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded a man that when he went to his bed he should recite the last verses of Surah al-Hashr, and he said: If you die, you die as a martyr.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever seeks refuge in Allah from Satan three times, then recites the last verses of Surah al-Hashr, Allah sends seventy angels who drive away from him the devils of mankind and jinn; if it is night, until morning, and if it is day, until evening."

Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Durays, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever says three times when he rises in the morning: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed, then recites the three verses from the end of Surah al-Hashr, Allah entrusts him to seventy thousand angels who send blessings upon him until evening; and if he dies that day, he dies a martyr. And whoever says it in the evening has the same rank."

Al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: Gharib (strange); we do not know it except through this route.

Ibn Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the final verses of al-Hashr at night or by day, and dies that same day or night, Allah makes Paradise obligatory for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that he said: the secret and the open. And regarding His saying: ﴿Al-Mu'min﴾, he said: the One who grants His creation safety from wronging them. And regarding His saying: ﴿Al-Muhaymin﴾, he said: the Witness.

It has been said: the One who confirms the believers in what He has promised them of reward and confirms the disbelievers in what He has threatened them with of punishment. It is said: amanahu (he granted him security) from al-amn, which is the opposite of fear. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And the Believer (al-mu'min), whose sanctuaries the birds wipe, the riders of Makkah between al-Ghayl and al-Sanad."

Mujahid said: al-Mu'min is the One who affirmed His own oneness by His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾.

Al-Jumhur read al-Mu'min with a kasra on the mim, an active participle from amana, in the sense of amina (to be secure).

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn read it with a fatha, in the sense of al-mu'man bihi (the one believed in), by elision, like His saying: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf 155]. Abu Hatim said: this reading is not permissible, because its meaning would be that he was fearful and someone else granted him security.

﴿Al-Muhaymin﴾: that is, the Witness over His servants regarding their deeds, the Watcher over them. Thus said Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil: it is said haymana yuhaymin, so he is muhaymin, when he is a watcher over a thing.

Al-Wahidi said: many of the exegetes held that its origin is mu'ayman, from amana yu'minu, so it would mean al-mu'min, but the first view is better. We have already discussed al-muhaymin in Surah al-Ma'idah.

﴿Al-'Aziz﴾: the One who has no equal. It has been said: the Subduer. It has been said: the Victorious, who is not overcome. It has been said: the Strong, the Compeller. Jabbar: the majesty of Allah is His greatness. The Arabs call a king jabbar. It may also be from jabara, when he enriches the poor and mends the broken. It may also be from jabarahu ʿala kadhā, when he compels him to what he wills; so He is the One who compelled His creation to what He wills from them. This was the view of al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Zajjaj preferred it, and al-Farra' said: it is from ajbarahu ʿala al-amr, meaning he forced him to it. He said: I have not heard fa''āl from af'ala except in jabbār from ajbara, and darrāk from adraka. It has also been said: al-Jabbar is the One whose might cannot be withstood.

﴿Al-Mutakabbir﴾: that is, the One who is exalted above every deficiency and magnified beyond what is not fitting for Him. The root of takabbur is refusal and not submitting. From it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"It has been effaced as the weaned calf effaces, and in it has become the pride of the stubborn, and it is now tame."

Pride (al-kibr) in the attributes of Allah is praise, and in the attributes of created beings it is blame.

Qatadah said: He is the One who is exalted above every evil.

Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Mutakabbir: the Possessor of greatness, who is the King.

Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the associating of the polytheists, so He said: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate﴾: that is, above what they associate with Him, or above their associating [others] with Him.

﴿He is Allah, the Creator﴾: that is, the One who determines things according to the requirement of His will and purpose. ﴿The Originator﴾: that is, the One who brings things into being, innovates them, and makes them exist. It has been said: the One who distinguishes some of them from others. ﴿The Fashioner﴾: that is, the One who brings forms into existence and composes them in various shapes. Tasywir (fashioning) follows upon khalq (creation) and bara' (origination) and is subsequent to them. The meaning of tasywir is outlining and shaping. Al-Nabigha said:

"The Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner in the wombs, from water until it becomes blood."

Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a Companion, read al-muṣawwar with a fatha on the waw and a fatha on the ra', as the object of al-bari' (the Originator): that is, the One who originated the fashioned one, meaning, He distinguished it.

﴿To Him belong the best names﴾: its explanation and discussion have already preceded in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the best names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 180].

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾: that is, whatever is in them declares Him free from imperfection, by the tongue of state or of speech. ﴿And He is the Almighty, the Wise﴾: that is, the Victorious over others, whom none can overcome, the Wise in all the matters by which He decrees.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾, that he said: it means, "Had I sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, which I had made it bear, it would have split and humbled itself from its weight and from the fear of Allah." So Allah commanded the people, when the Qur'an is revealed to them, to receive it with intense fear and humility. He said: Thus does Allah set forth parables for the people, that perhaps they may give thought.

(p-1481) Al-Daylami related from Ibn Mas'ud and Ali, in a marfu' report, regarding His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ to the end of the surah, that he said: it is a remedy for headache.

Al-Daylami narrated it with two chains, and we do not know the condition of their narrators.

Al-Khatib (al-Baghdadi) related in his History, with his chain, to Idris ibn Abd al-Karim al-Haddad, who said: I read to Khalaf, and when I reached this verse he said: Place your hand on your head, for I read to Hamzah, and when I reached this verse he said: Place your hand on your head, for I read to al-A'mash. Then he continued the chain in this manner, linked (musalsal), to Ibn Mas'ud, who said: I read to the Prophet ﷺ, and when I reached this verse he said to me: Place your hand on your head, for when Jibril descended with it, he said to me: Place your hand on your head, for it is a cure for every disease except al-sam, and al-sam is death.

Al-Dhahabi said: this is false.

Ibn al-Sunni in ʿAmal al-Yawm wa al-Layla and Ibn Mardawayh also related, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded a man that when he went to his bed he should recite the last verses of Surah al-Hashr, and he said: If you die, you die as a martyr.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever seeks refuge in Allah from Satan three times, then recites the last verses of Surah al-Hashr, Allah sends seventy angels who drive away from him the devils of mankind and jinn; if it is night, until morning, and if it is day, until evening."

Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Durays, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever says three times when he rises in the morning: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed, then recites the three verses from the end of Surah al-Hashr, Allah entrusts him to seventy thousand angels who send blessings upon him until evening; and if he dies that day, he dies a martyr. And whoever says it in the evening has the same rank."

Al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: Gharib (strange); we do not know it except through this route.

Ibn Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the final verses of al-Hashr at night or by day, and dies that same day or night, Allah makes Paradise obligatory for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that he said: the secret and the open. And regarding His saying: ﴿Al-Mu'min﴾, he said: the One who grants His creation safety from wronging them. And regarding His saying: ﴿Al-Muhaymin﴾, he said: the Witness.
